passage.title: Why Coral Restoration Is Not Simply Gardening

paragraphs.text: Coral restoration has developed beyond repairing damage at a single location to include growing corals in nurseries and placing them on degraded reefs. The activity can resemble gardening: workers raise small pieces, attach them carefully, and return to check their growth. Imagine such a project several months after planting. Most of the corals remain attached, and their living tissue has spread. For the team that transported and secured them, this is encouraging evidence. Yet what, precisely, has succeeded? The answer depends on whether the team is describing a planting operation, a coral population, or the wider reef.

Establishment means that planted corals have survived the immediate difficulties of transfer and begun living at the chosen site. Population recovery asks a different question: can corals persist and produce new generations there? Ecosystem recovery reaches further, considering relationships among corals, other organisms, and their physical surroundings. These categories overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A reef cannot recover without living corals, although a collection of living corals does not by itself demonstrate a recovering reef. This distinction matters when a photograph of healthy new growth is used to support a much broader claim about restoration.

The boundary becomes clearer when conditions change outside the planting area. Unusually warm water can cause corals to lose the algae living within their tissues, producing the pale appearance called bleaching. Bleaching does not necessarily mean immediate death, but prolonged stress can threaten survival. Successfully attached corals remain exposed to this pressure. Water carrying pollution or sediment can also enter from beyond a project's boundary. A later decline therefore does not automatically reveal poor planting technique. Equally, careful planting cannot be treated as evidence that the environmental pressures responsible for earlier losses have disappeared.

Different measurements reveal different parts of this picture. Survival records show how many planted corals remain alive. Growth measurements add information about their condition, while evidence of reproduction and the survival of young corals can indicate whether a population is renewing itself. Recording several species provides information that a count of numerous individuals of one species cannot supply. None of these observations should simply replace the others. Reproduction without successful survival of the next generation leaves an important gap; high survival among a narrow selection of corals may conceal limited diversity. The useful question is what each measurement permits observers to conclude. Consider two hypothetical sites with equal numbers of surviving corals. At one, workers repeatedly replace losses with nursery material; at the other, young corals survive without those additions. The totals may look alike, yet they describe different dependence on continued human effort. Recording the source of new individuals makes that difference visible to evaluators.

Local protection still has a meaningful role. Reducing damage from boats or improving nearby water quality can remove pressures that restoration workers are able to influence. Such measures may give planted corals a better opportunity to survive and grow. They cannot, however, keep a large region of ocean cool during an extended period of heat. Treating local action as a complete response confuses its geographical reach with its value. The opposite judgment is also mistaken: the existence of a wider threat does not show that every avoidable local injury is unimportant. Both scales can affect the same coral at the same time.

A credible assessment therefore follows several measures over multiple years and records the conditions under which changes occur. Comparable sites without planting can help assess whether improvements reflect the intervention or a generally favorable period, although differences between sites must also be considered. Reports should preserve narrower achievements even when broader goals remain uncertain. A team may have established corals successfully without yet demonstrating population recovery, and a population may improve without the whole ecosystem returning to its former condition. These are meaningful distinctions, not merely cautious wording. They allow restoration's actual contribution to be recognized while leaving its long term outcome open to evidence.

questions.stem: Why is the early growth in the imagined project insufficient to establish that the reef has recovered?

choices.text: It suggests that future assessment should concentrate on tissue growth instead of the original planting.
choices.text_ja: 今後の評価は、最初の植え付けではなく組織の成長に集中すべきだと示唆しているから。

choices.text: It shows that the planted individuals have grown, suggesting that further population measures can focus on species numbers.
choices.text_ja: 植え付けた個体が成長したことを示しており、今後の個体群の測定は種の数に絞ってよいと示唆しているから。

choices.text: The growth mainly indicates that the surrounding reef already supported a renewing population.
choices.text_ja: その成長は主に、周囲のサンゴ礁がすでに自ら更新する個体群を支えていたことを示しているから。

choices.text: It demonstrates one stage of progress without establishing the wider relationships involved in recovery.
choices.text_ja: 進展の一段階を示してはいるが、回復に関わるより広い関係までは立証していないから。

questions.stem: Suppose planted corals decline during regional warming despite improved local water quality. Which interpretation best fits the passage?
questions.stem_ja: 地域の水質が改善したにもかかわらず、広域的な水温上昇の間に植え付けたサンゴが減少したとする。本文の内容に最もよく合う解釈はどれか。

choices.text: The decline suggests that initial survival records overstated how well the corals handled transplantation.
choices.text_ja: その減少は、初期の生存の記録が、サンゴが移植にうまく対応した度合いを過大に示していたことを示唆している。

choices.text: The decline indicates that water quality improvements had little relevance before the warming began.
choices.text_ja: その減少は、水温上昇が始まる前には水質の改善がほとんど関係なかったことを示している。

choices.text: The corals may have benefited locally while remaining exposed to a pressure beyond local control.
choices.text_ja: サンゴは地域での対策の恩恵を受けていたかもしれないが、地域では制御できない圧力にさらされ続けていた。

choices.text: The regional event provides evidence that the corals had failed to establish after transfer.
choices.text_ja: 広域的な出来事は、移植後にサンゴが定着できていなかったことの証拠となる。

questions.stem: Which finding would most directly strengthen a claim of population recovery beyond initial establishment?
questions.stem_ja: 最初の定着を超えて、個体群が回復したという主張を最も直接的に強める発見はどれか。

choices.text: Photographs show greater tissue coverage among the original planted corals.
choices.text_ja: 写真から、最初に植え付けたサンゴの組織の被覆が広がっていることが分かる。

choices.text: Workers plant additional individuals of several species in the same area.
choices.text_ja: 作業員が同じ区域に、いくつかの種の個体を追加で植え付ける。

choices.text: New corals produced at the site survive and become part of the population.
choices.text_ja: その場所で生まれた新しいサンゴが生き残り、個体群の一部になる。

choices.text: A larger proportion of transplanted pieces remain firmly attached after transfer.
choices.text_ja: 移植した断片のうち、移植後もしっかり固定されたままのものの割合が高くなる。

questions.stem: Which reporting practice would best follow the author's approach?
questions.stem_ja: 筆者の考え方に最もよく沿った報告の仕方はどれか。

choices.text: Delay recognition of successful planting until the reef resembles its former ecosystem.
choices.text_ja: サンゴ礁がかつての生態系に近い状態になるまで、植え付けの成功を認めるのを控える。

choices.text: Describe what each measure supports and distinguish achieved stages from uncertain outcomes.
choices.text_ja: それぞれの指標が何を裏づけるかを説明し、達成された段階と不確かな結果とを区別する。

choices.text: Give reproduction records priority over survival data when the two suggest different trends.
choices.text_ja: 繁殖の記録と生存のデータが異なる傾向を示す場合は、繁殖の記録を優先する。

choices.text: Use the strongest improving measure to give each project a consistent overall success rating.
choices.text_ja: 最も改善している指標を使って、各プロジェクトに一貫した総合的な成功評価を与える。

questions.stem: Why should evaluators consider differences between planted and unplanted sites?
questions.stem_ja: 評価する人が、植え付けを行った場所と行っていない場所の違いを考慮すべきなのはなぜか。

choices.text: They may offer another explanation for changes attributed to the planting intervention.
choices.text_ja: 植え付けという介入によるとされた変化について、別の説明となりうるから。

choices.text: They show whether establishment should be classified as an ecosystem measure.
choices.text_ja: 定着を生態系の指標に分類すべきかどうかを示すから。

choices.text: Those differences identify which growth measures can replace long term observation.
choices.text_ja: それらの違いから、どの成長の指標が長期的な観察の代わりになるかが分かるから。

choices.text: They determine whether narrower planting achievements deserve to be reported.
choices.text_ja: より限られた植え付けの成果を報告する価値があるかどうかを決めるから。

passage.title: The Reliability of Eyewitness Confidence

paragraphs.text: As methods for recording events have expanded, eyewitness accounts can increasingly be compared with evidence independent of the speaker's memory. The comparison can be uncomfortable. Imagine a witness describing a person with complete confidence, while a recording shows that one remembered detail is wrong. The witness may be sincere, and the account may contain other accurate details. The disagreement nevertheless raises a question: what does confidence tell an evaluator? Answering requires a distinction between the event a person originally experienced and the later process through which that experience becomes an account told to others.

Memory accuracy concerns how well an account matches what happened. Confidence concerns how strongly the person believes that account. The two can be related, but they are not identical measures. An evaluator who hears a clear, fluent description may be receiving information about both the original observation and everything that occurred afterward. A witness can remember an event vividly while being mistaken about a feature within it. Conversely, someone who speaks cautiously may be responding to poor viewing conditions rather than admitting that every remembered detail is unreliable. The manner of presentation cannot settle the accuracy of each claim.

Questions are part of the later process. Compare asking what a witness noticed about a vehicle with asking about its broken window. The second question introduces a detail that the witness may not have independently reported. Repeated discussion can make suggested information familiar, complicating the task of separating what was seen from what was later heard. This does not mean that every repeated question changes memory or that a follow-up interview is useless. It means the wording and sequence of questions can become relevant evidence when evaluating the eventual account. A final answer alone leaves that history out.

Feedback can also change the meaning of confidence. Suppose a witness selects someone from a set of photographs, expresses uncertainty, and then receives approving comments. If the witness later speaks with greater certainty, that increase is not a new observation of the original event. It may partly reflect the response to the selection. Confidence recorded at the first identification, before feedback, is therefore different evidence from confidence expressed much later. The earlier statement is not automatically correct; it is useful because one potential source of later influence has not yet entered the record.

These distinctions suggest procedures that preserve information instead of simply asking evaluators to distrust confident people. An interviewer can first invite an account without supplying disputed details. The questions, answers, and initial expression of confidence can be recorded as closely as possible to the witness's own words. When arranging an identification procedure, keeping the person who administers it unaware of which individual is suspected can reduce opportunities for unintended cues. These measures address different sources of influence. Recording uncertainty documents it; avoiding cues helps prevent additional influence. One measure cannot fully perform the other's function.

Independent evidence remains important throughout. If a later account conflicts with a recording, an evaluator should examine the particular disagreement and the history of questioning, rather than classify the witness as wholly truthful or wholly unreliable. A recording of an interview documents what was said and how it was elicited; it does not itself verify the original event. Likewise, agreement between two witnesses needs interpretation if they discussed their memories together. Their matching accounts may contain less independent support than matching accounts produced separately before such discussion.

The opening question consequently has a conditional answer. Confidence can contribute to an assessment when its timing and the conditions under which it was expressed are known. Later certainty detached from that history deserves a different interpretation. Good procedures do not turn human memory into a recording device. They make it easier to distinguish the information a witness initially supplied from influences that may have shaped its presentation, allowing testimony to be evaluated more carefully rather than accepted or rejected as a single package.

questions.stem: What does the imagined disagreement with a recording establish?
questions.stem_ja: 記録映像との食い違いを想定した例は、何を示しているか。

choices.text: The witness's confidence mainly reflects later questioning rather than the original event.
choices.text_ja: 目撃者の確信は、もとの出来事よりも、主に後の質問を反映している。

choices.text: The inaccurate detail makes the remaining description unsuitable for further evaluation.
choices.text_ja: 不正確な細部があるため、説明の残りの部分はそれ以上評価するのに適さない。

choices.text: A cautious account would provide stronger evidence than the confident account.
choices.text_ja: 慎重な証言のほうが、自信に満ちた証言よりも強い証拠となる。

choices.text: Sincere confidence can accompany an error within an otherwise partly accurate account.
choices.text_ja: ほかの部分はある程度正確な証言の中でも、誠実な確信が誤りを伴うことがある。

questions.stem: Why is asking about a broken window different from asking what the witness noticed?
questions.stem_ja: 割れた窓について尋ねることが、目撃者が何に気づいたかを尋ねることと異なるのはなぜか。

choices.text: It focuses on a small detail that is less likely to matter in a later evaluation.
choices.text_ja: 後の評価で重要になる可能性が低い、小さな細部に焦点を当てているから。

choices.text: It repeats the original scene in a way that strengthens the witness's access to it.
choices.text_ja: もとの場面を再現することで、目撃者がその記憶を思い出しやすくなるから。

choices.text: It makes the response more precise and therefore easier to verify without other evidence.
choices.text_ja: 答えがより正確になり、そのためほかの証拠がなくても検証しやすくなるから。

choices.text: It introduces information that may become mixed with the witness's own observation.
choices.text_ja: 目撃者自身の観察と混ざりかねない情報を持ち込んでいるから。

questions.stem: Why record confidence at the initial identification?
questions.stem_ja: 最初の識別の時点で確信の程度を記録するのはなぜか。

choices.text: It reduces the need to keep the administrator unaware of the suspected person.
choices.text_ja: 実施担当者に容疑者を知らせないでおく必要性が減るから。

choices.text: It preserves a judgment made before later feedback could influence certainty.
choices.text_ja: 後の反応が確信に影響を与える前に下された判断を保存できるから。

choices.text: It establishes a fixed level of accuracy that later interviews can be compared against.
choices.text_ja: 後の聞き取りと比較できる、正確さの固定した基準が定まるから。

choices.text: It helps the interviewer choose which encouraging comments will be appropriate afterward.
choices.text_ja: 聞き取りをする人が、その後どのような励ましのコメントが適切かを選びやすくなるから。

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of an interview recording?
questions.stem_ja: 聞き取りの録音・録画の主な限界は何か。

choices.text: It preserves the initial wording but provides little information about the interviewer's questions.
choices.text_ja: 最初の言葉づかいは保存されるが、聞き取りをする人の質問についてはほとんど情報が得られない。

choices.text: It documents procedural influences but makes independent event evidence less useful.
choices.text_ja: 手続き上の影響は記録されるが、出来事に関する独立した証拠の有用性が下がる。

choices.text: It shows how testimony was obtained without directly establishing what originally happened.
choices.text_ja: 証言がどのように得られたかは示されるが、もともと何が起きたのかを直接立証するわけではない。

choices.text: It gives a reliable account of the original scene if the interview begins with open questions.
choices.text_ja: 聞き取りが自由回答式の質問から始まれば、もとの場面について信頼できる説明が得られる。

questions.stem: Two witnesses give matching confident accounts after discussing the event. How should an evaluator treat the match?
questions.stem_ja: 二人の目撃者が、出来事について話し合った後に、自信に満ちた一致する証言をした。評価者はこの一致をどう扱うべきか。

choices.text: As possible support whose independence is uncertain because the accounts may have influenced each other.
choices.text_ja: 裏づけになりうるが、証言が互いに影響し合った可能性があるため、その独立性は不確かなものとして扱う。

choices.text: As equivalent to separate initial accounts if the witnesses express the same degree of confidence.
choices.text_ja: 二人が同じ程度の確信を示しているなら、別々に得られた最初の証言と同等のものとして扱う。

choices.text: As stronger evidence of accurate observation because both witnesses had time to reconsider.
choices.text_ja: 二人とも考え直す時間があったので、正確な観察を示すより強い証拠として扱う。

choices.text: As evidence mainly about the interview procedure, with little relevance to the original event.
choices.text_ja: 主に聞き取りの手続きに関する証拠であり、もとの出来事とはほとんど関係がないものとして扱う。

passage.title: The Administrative Logic of Ancient Canals

paragraphs.text: As ancient settlements expanded into cities, waterways could become connections between cultivated land, storage areas, and growing urban populations. In Mesopotamia, canals formed part of this changing landscape, supplying water and supporting movement. Their remains invite a familiar explanation: people dug them to irrigate fields. That explanation has considerable force, but a canal's position may raise further questions. Why might a channel approach a market or pass a group of large buildings before reaching farmland? Understanding such arrangements requires distinguishing what a surviving channel makes possible from what people demonstrably used it to do.

Irrigation offers a sensible starting hypothesis. A canal can carry water away from a river toward land that otherwise receives too little. A branch leading into fields is therefore consistent with agricultural use. Yet consistency is not exclusive proof. The same channel may have supported boats along part of its length, and the goods they carried may themselves have come from those fields. Calling one function agricultural and another commercial can separate activities that were closely connected in practice. Even where irrigation is well supported, it need not explain every feature of a canal's route or management.

Consider a hypothetical ancient city with a canal joining fields to a cluster of storehouses near a market. This arrangement could have made it easier to transport crops and collect deliveries at a limited number of points. Officials might have used those points to record goods or collect obligations owed to an authority. Such an interpretation explains why access and oversight could matter alongside water supply. It remains a hypothesis, however. A convenient place for collecting goods does not by itself prove that a tax was collected there, or identify the institution responsible for doing so.

Other features raise questions about water control. Channels and their banks can direct water, so their maintenance may relate to protecting occupied areas as well as supplying fields. Whether a particular canal reduced flood danger depends on its design and local conditions; its presence alone is insufficient. The practical demands also create an administrative issue. Clearing accumulated material or repairing a bank requires labor, timing, and decisions about priorities. Written records of workers and supervisors can illuminate those arrangements. They may reveal organized maintenance more directly than they reveal the complete purpose for which a canal was first constructed.

Different kinds of evidence thus carry different limits. Terrain shows where water could flow, while traces of buildings suggest where goods or people may have gathered. An inscription may name a ruler associated with digging a canal, but the ruler's chosen description need not list every everyday use. A record of deliveries near a channel can support an interpretation involving transport, especially when the physical setting fits. Combining these sources can strengthen an explanation because each addresses a different uncertainty. Combining them carelessly can instead produce a detailed story whose separate parts never actually belong together.

Time is one reason the parts may not fit. A canal could have been extended, redirected, or used differently as a city developed. A storehouse beside its surviving route might date from a later period than its original construction. In that case, the building could support later commercial use without explaining the first route. Evaluators need to ask not merely whether two remains are close, but whether their periods of use overlap. Otherwise, a map containing many centuries of evidence can misleadingly resemble a single plan created at one moment.

The most defensible interpretation is therefore often layered. Irrigation, movement of goods, water control, and organized labor can belong to the same system, while their relative importance varies across places and periods. An individual canal still requires evidence for each claimed role. What can be rejected is the assumption that identifying one useful function completes the explanation. Canals were physical channels embedded in urban arrangements; reconstructing those arrangements requires both broader questions and precise limits on what the surviving evidence can establish.

choices.text: It supports irrigation while leaving room for related transport and management functions.

choices.text: It indicates that commercial traffic was less important than agricultural water supply.

questions.stem: Which additional evidence would most directly strengthen the tax-collection interpretation in the hypothetical city?
questions.stem_ja: 仮想の都市における徴税の解釈を最も直接的に裏づける追加の証拠はどれか。

choices.text: A wider channel capable of carrying boats toward the storehouses.
choices.text_ja: 貯蔵庫に向けて船を通せるほど幅の広い水路。

choices.text: Repairs indicating repeated maintenance of the route near the market.
choices.text_ja: 市場付近の経路が繰り返し維持管理されていたことを示す補修の跡。

choices.text: Records linking deliveries at those storehouses to obligations owed to an authority.
choices.text_ja: それらの貯蔵庫への納入を、権力者に納めるべきものと結びつける記録。

choices.text: Field boundaries showing that several farms could use the same branch.
choices.text_ja: 複数の農場が同じ支流を利用できたことを示す畑の境界。

questions.stem: How do worker records and terrain evidence differ in what they most directly reveal?
questions.stem_ja: 労働者の記録と地形の証拠とでは、最も直接的に明らかにするものがどう異なるか。

choices.text: Worker records illuminate organized labor, while terrain indicates possible water movement.
choices.text_ja: 労働者の記録は組織的な労働を明らかにし、地形は水が流れえた経路を示す。

choices.text: Worker records establish original design, while terrain shows changes in political authority.
choices.text_ja: 労働者の記録は当初の設計を立証し、地形は政治権力の変化を示す。

choices.text: Worker records explain flood protection, while terrain identifies the goods carried by boats.
choices.text_ja: 労働者の記録は洪水対策を説明し、地形は船で運ばれた物資を特定する。

choices.text: Worker records establish commercial use, while terrain identifies who ordered construction.
choices.text_ja: 労働者の記録は商業的な利用を立証し、地形は建設を命じた人物を特定する。

questions.stem: A storehouse beside a canal was built long after the canal's first construction. What follows?
questions.stem_ja: 運河の脇にある貯蔵庫が、運河が最初に建設されてからかなり後に建てられたものだった。ここから何が言えるか。

choices.text: The canal's position can date the storehouse more reliably than the building evidence can.
choices.text_ja: 運河の位置のほうが、建物の証拠よりも確実に貯蔵庫の年代を特定できる。

choices.text: The canal probably changed from irrigation to transport when the storehouse was built.
choices.text_ja: 貯蔵庫が建てられた時点で、運河はおそらく灌漑用から輸送用に変わった。

choices.text: Its location is weak evidence for later canal use because the original builders did not plan it.
choices.text_ja: 当初の建設者が計画したものではないので、その位置は後の運河の利用を示す証拠としては弱い。

choices.text: It may support later commercial use without explaining the canal's original route.
choices.text_ja: それは後の時代の商業的な利用を裏づけうるが、運河の当初の経路を説明するものではない。

questions.stem: Why does the author favor a layered interpretation?
questions.stem_ja: 筆者が何層にも重なった解釈を支持するのはなぜか。

choices.text: A broad urban account can fill gaps where individual sources supply little detail.
choices.text_ja: 都市全体についての幅広い説明によって、個々の資料がほとんど詳細を示さない部分の空白を埋められるから。

choices.text: Multiple possible uses make it reasonable to assign the same functions to neighboring canals.
choices.text_ja: 複数の用途がありうるので、隣接する運河にも同じ機能を当てはめるのが妥当だから。

choices.text_ja: 管理に関する証拠のほうが、地形の分析よりも効果的に物理的な不確かさを解消できるから。

passage.title: A Cooperative's Dilemma Over Fair Prices

paragraphs.text: Could the fictional Vale Growers Cooperative continue guaranteeing the same minimum purchase price if membership doubled? Its board could examine that question through records of purchases, sales, and reserves. The question mattered because the guarantee had become central to what members called fair treatment. Whenever the market price fell below the promised amount, the cooperative paid growers the difference from a shared fund. The promise covered all accepted produce, with quality requirements agreed in advance. It offered a clear rule, but the resources needed to apply that rule depended on how much produce the cooperative accepted.

At a small farm supplying the cooperative, the guarantee changed the owner's planning. A known minimum made it easier to estimate whether basic costs could be met before planting. The owner still faced weather risks and quality requirements, yet one source of uncertainty had been reduced. From this viewpoint, lowering the guarantee after attracting new members would feel like changing the terms of cooperation. A rule that gave every accepted unit of produce the same protection also seemed impartial. Larger and smaller suppliers received the same minimum for comparable goods, rather than bargaining separately with the buyer.

At the cooperative's packing building, the accounts presented another view. New members brought more produce during a period when selling prices were weak. Each unit sold below the guaranteed purchase price required support from the reserve. A larger membership did not automatically bring enough additional income to cover that gap. Raising the price charged to shops was one option, but buyers could reduce their orders or turn to other suppliers. Protecting the payment on each unit might then make it harder to sell the total harvest, increasing storage costs and leaving less money for future guarantees.

Back at the small farm, a proposal to limit guaranteed purchases received a mixed response. Under this proposal, each member would receive the full guarantee for an initial quantity, with additional produce bought at the market price. Smaller suppliers welcomed protection concentrated on their basic sales. Larger suppliers argued that they had made investments on the understanding that comparable produce would receive comparable treatment. A limit could spread a fixed fund across more households, yet it would move away from equal treatment of every unit. Both descriptions could be accurate because they used different units of fairness: households and quantities.

The board then considered a lower universal guarantee combined with an additional payment when annual sales went well. This would preserve a common price rule and reduce pressure on reserves in poor periods. At the small farm, however, a possible later payment could not fully replace a dependable minimum when planning essential expenses. Shop buyers, meanwhile, valued a supplier that could continue operating and deliver consistently. They did not necessarily share the growers' preference for the highest immediate purchase price. The cooperative had to consider relationships over time as well as the distribution of this season's income.

No proposal removed the need to decide what the shared fund was meant to protect. The board modeled each option using the same sales assumptions, then asked how results changed if buyers ordered less. It also separated commitments already made from terms offered for the next season, so a financial redesign would not be confused with silently changing existing promises. These steps made the consequences easier to compare. They could estimate how long reserves might last and which members would receive most support, but the calculations could not decide whether equal support per household was preferable to equal support per unit.

The original question thus led to more than a balance-sheet answer. The accounts showed that extending the existing promise required resources that membership growth alone did not supply. Calling a replacement policy fair required a further judgment about whose security, which comparisons, and what period mattered. The cooperative's task was to state that judgment openly and connect it to a financially workable promise, rather than present a changed price rule as though the meaning of fairness had remained untouched.

passage.title: Why Some Languages Lose Distinctions

paragraphs.text: What would show that two generations no longer use the same sound distinction? Imagine recordings in which older speakers consistently give two words different vowel sounds, while younger speakers pronounce the words alike. This is a hypothetical example, but it identifies a question that can be investigated by comparing speech. The words may retain different spellings and meanings even when their pronunciations become identical. A listener might describe the change as careless speech or a general move toward easier pronunciation. Those descriptions go beyond the observed difference and require explanations of their own.

A sound distinction matters when it helps separate words. If two formerly contrasting sounds become one in the same circumstances, linguists describe the change as a merger. The important fact is a change in the relationship between sounds, not merely a change in one person's voice. A speaker might pronounce both vowels somewhat differently from an older speaker while continuing to keep them apart. In that case, their sounds have changed without the contrast disappearing. To demonstrate a merger, an investigator needs evidence about the distinction across relevant words, rather than one striking pronunciation recorded in isolation.

Ease of pronunciation can be relevant to sound change, but it is not a complete explanation for every lost contrast. Speech involves moving between sounds, so the position of the tongue or lips for a neighboring sound can influence pronunciation. A distinction may disappear in one environment while remaining in another. Calling the result simpler does not explain why that particular environment mattered. It also says little about changes elsewhere in the language that create new differences. Counting fewer contrasts in a selected group of words cannot establish that the language as a whole has become easier to speak or learn.

Contact between speakers provides another possible influence. People regularly hear different ways of pronouncing words, whether from another language or another variety of their own. Some forms may spread through social interaction. Yet the presence of contact does not prove that it caused a particular merger: a similar outcome could develop through changes within the sound system. Evidence about where and when a pronunciation appears can help compare these explanations. If a proposed outside source acquired the feature later than the receiving community, for example, the proposed direction of influence would need reconsideration.

The words themselves also matter to the investigation. A pattern found in a few frequently used words may not yet describe the entire sound system. Investigators can compare common and less common words, different neighboring sounds, and speech produced in different situations. If a speaker separates the sounds when reading carefully but brings them together in ordinary conversation, describing the contrast as simply present or absent may hide useful information. The evidence could indicate variation that deserves further study. It should not be forced into a completed historical change merely because a short recording gives that impression.

Losing one distinction does not prevent new contrasts from developing elsewhere. Consider an illustrative possibility: a vowel first sounds different because of a following consonant. If that consonant later disappears, the vowel difference may remain and begin distinguishing words on its own. This is not a claim that every merger is balanced by a new contrast. It shows why examining the whole system can reveal a reorganization that a list of disappearing sounds would miss. Speakers also use the surrounding sentence to interpret words, so identical pronunciations need not make every conversation confusing.

The initial recordings would therefore support a carefully bounded observation: the sampled speakers treated particular words differently across generations. Establishing how widely the contrast was lost, why it changed, and what happened elsewhere requires additional comparisons. A language is more than an inventory of separate sounds; its words and patterns connect those sounds to one another. Describing those connections allows a change to be explained without turning the loss of one distinction into a judgment that later speakers are less precise or their entire language is simpler.

passage.title: The Limits of a Perfect Solar Panel

paragraphs.text: How should two solar panels be compared if one converts a larger share of incoming light into electricity but costs more to make? Efficiency provides a precise starting point: it relates electrical output to the light energy received. It does not, by itself, answer every question about installing a panel. Even a highly efficient device leaves some incoming energy unused as electricity. Understanding why requires looking inside the conversion process, then returning to the scale of an entire installation. A laboratory achievement and a practical purchasing decision involve connected measurements, but they are not the same evaluation.

Sunlight contains light of different wavelengths, corresponding to different amounts of energy carried by individual photons, the packets in which light interacts with matter. A solar cell's material responds to these photons according to its properties. In a simplified description, a photon needs enough energy to enable an electron to move into a state that can contribute to electrical current. The required energy difference is called the band gap. Photons below that threshold cannot drive this process in the same way. Choosing a material therefore involves choosing a particular response to the range of incoming light.

The threshold creates a tradeoff. A material with a smaller band gap can use a wider range of lower-energy photons, but that does not mean it converts all the energy in higher-energy photons into electricity. Energy above what the process can use is partly lost as heat. A larger band gap changes the balance, leaving more low-energy photons unused while potentially obtaining more electrical energy from suitable absorbed photons. The two kinds of loss cannot both be removed merely by selecting a single threshold more carefully. This is one reason a well-made cell can still fall short of complete conversion.

One approach is to divide the work among materials. A multijunction cell uses layers with different band gaps so that different parts of the incoming light can be used more effectively. The arrangement can raise efficiency compared with relying on one suitable material. However, its layers must be manufactured and combined successfully, and additional complexity can increase costs. The benefit also depends on the design and the conditions in which it operates. Saying that several materials use sunlight more effectively explains a technical advantage; it does not establish that every such device is the best choice for every installation.

At the laboratory scale, carefully specified conditions allow meaningful comparisons between devices. At the building scale, the question becomes how much electricity a complete system supplies over time. Shade, temperature, orientation, and changing sunlight can affect that result. Components connecting the panels to the electrical system matter as well. A record efficiency measured for a cell does not directly describe the annual output of a rooftop installation. The laboratory measurement remains valuable, but using it for a building requires information about the product and the setting in which it will be used.

Consider two hypothetical buildings. One has a small roof and strong demand for electricity; making better use of each available area may justify paying more for efficiency. The other has ample suitable space but a tight budget. A less efficient option may supply the required electricity at a lower total cost there. Neither comparison can be resolved by panel price alone, since installation, maintenance, and service life also matter. Nor does the example imply that the cheaper option necessarily wins on the larger roof. It identifies the additional information needed before choosing between proposals.

A useful evaluation thus keeps its measures attached to their questions. Conversion efficiency describes how effectively a device uses incoming light under stated conditions. Energy supplied over time describes a system's contribution in a location. Cost and durability help determine whether that contribution meets the user's needs. Improving efficiency remains a real technical achievement, while maximizing it is not automatically the same as finding the most suitable installation. The limits arise partly from how materials handle light and partly from the wider decision the word 'best' is being asked to express.

passage.title: When Evacuation Maps Mislead

paragraphs.text: In the fictional coastal city of Marrow Bay, a household inside a shaded hazard area reached the practice shelter promptly, while another household outside the shading arrived much later. The second home was closer to the shelter on the printed map. During the city's evacuation exercise, however, its usual bridge was treated as closed, forcing a long detour. The contrast surprised residents who had used their home's position relative to the colored boundary as a measure of their situation. Why had the apparently less exposed household faced the harder journey? The exercise gave planners a way to separate several kinds of information.

The map's shaded area represented locations expected to face a particular hazard under the scenario used to produce it. This was useful information about exposure, not a promise about every possible event. The map also showed streets and designated shelters. A line connecting a home to a shelter could look straightforward on paper even if part of it crossed the hazard area. Moreover, the printed sheet could not show whether a road was open at the moment someone needed it. The location of a house and the condition of its route answered different questions, although both appeared on the same surface.

The bridge in the exercise made that difference concrete. Before the simulated closure, the shorter route was available; afterward, its value changed abruptly. The detour required more time even though neither the home nor the shelter had moved. Departure time therefore affected which route could be used and how long the journey took. Planners were careful not to treat the exercise's timing as a prediction of a future event. Its value was to reveal dependence on one crossing and to ask what alternatives existed if that crossing became unavailable.

Travel method introduced a second difference within the same neighborhood. A route that accommodated a pedestrian group included steps unsuitable for a resident using a wheelchair. The driving route avoided the steps but joined a road where the exercise produced a queue. Families comparing their journeys initially described one route as faster, until planners asked for whom and under which conditions. A route's length did not capture accessibility, traffic, or the time needed to prepare assistance. Nor could the successful journey of one household establish that its neighbors had an equally workable plan.

Residents still needed a readable map. Adding every possible closure and personal circumstance would make a single printed sheet difficult to use, while removing the shading would discard valuable information. The city therefore paired the map with other activities. During neighborhood exercises, residents checked routes appropriate to their circumstances and identified points where alternatives were needed. The city also explained which official channels would communicate current instructions during a real event. The map supplied a common picture of locations; practice exposed practical dependencies; updates addressed conditions that could change after printing.

These additions required care in their own interpretation. A route completed successfully on a quiet practice day had been tested under those conditions, not certified for every future emergency. Likewise, receiving an update depended on residents being able to access and understand it. In the next exercise, planners included a discussion of how households would obtain official information if their usual channel was unavailable. This did not produce a perfect plan. It made previously hidden assumptions visible, allowing residents and officials to distinguish known arrangements from points that still needed work.

The late household's experience was consequently more informative than a simple complaint that the map was wrong. Its home remained outside the shaded area in the scenario, but its movement depended on a vulnerable connection and on when it departed. The lesson was to read the boundary for the question it answered and combine it with evidence about routes, people, and changing conditions. In Marrow Bay, the map became a starting point for planning rather than a complete judgment of safety. Its limits could be managed more effectively once the city stopped asking a static picture to describe an entire unfolding journey.

questions.stem: Why was calling one neighborhood route faster incomplete?

passage.title: The Promise and Bias of Standardized Tests

paragraphs.text: Two students can receive the same score after very different learning experiences. Imagine one who has practiced a test's question format repeatedly and another who encounters it for the first time. Their equal scores establish equal performance on that occasion under the scoring rules. Whether they demonstrate equal command of a broader subject is a further question. The example does not establish that either student knows more. It introduces a problem faced whenever a common test is used to compare people whose opportunities, language experiences, and familiarity with assessment differ.

Standardization has a genuine advantage. Giving students comparable tasks under specified conditions and applying common scoring rules reduces some differences that would arise if every teacher devised an unrelated assessment. A score can provide a shared reference where local descriptions are difficult to compare. If those rules were removed, judgments might depend more heavily on individual expectations or inconsistent standards. This is a reason to preserve useful common measures. It is not yet a reason to assume that everything influencing those measures belongs to the ability the test is meant to assess.

The intended ability is crucial. On a test of reading in a particular language, understanding that language is central to the task. On a test intended to assess mathematical reasoning, unnecessarily complex instructions could make language experience an additional obstacle. The same language demand can therefore have different significance depending on the purpose. Similarly, familiarity with a question format may help a student express existing knowledge, while extensive practice on narrow item patterns may improve performance without an equally broad improvement in understanding. Identifying an influence is only the beginning; evaluators must ask whether it is relevant to their intended conclusion.

Consider two possible responses to the opening students. One evaluator could treat their scores as interchangeable evidence for every decision. This would preserve a straightforward rule but overlook differences not captured by the test. Another could adjust the interpretation according to background. This might reveal barriers, yet it could also introduce assumptions about individuals based on the groups they belong to. Knowing that a student had less test practice does not tell an evaluator exactly how much the score would have changed with more practice. Context can improve interpretation without supplying a precise correction.

A second assessment may help if it contributes different evidence. For example, students might explain their reasoning on unfamiliar problems, using tasks carefully aligned with the same subject goals. Agreement between this work and the test would strengthen some conclusions; disagreement would indicate a need to investigate. Additional measures also have their own limitations. A teacher's judgment may vary across classrooms, and a polished project may reflect unequal access to help. Gathering more scores is not automatically the same as obtaining more independent information. The useful question is which uncertainty the extra measure addresses and what new uncertainty it introduces.

Reliability and fairness consequently require related but distinct inquiries. A measure can produce consistent results while repeatedly reflecting an irrelevant barrier. Improving consistency would then make the pattern more stable without removing that barrier. Conversely, a change intended to broaden access must still be examined for whether it preserves the ability being assessed. Simplifying unnecessary wording on a mathematics task has a different implication from removing essential reading demands on a reading test. Fairness cannot be judged simply by checking whether everyone saw identical words, and it cannot be inferred from a desired distribution of scores.

The equal scores at the beginning remain useful evidence about performance under common conditions. They do not erase differences in experience, nor do those differences prove unequal underlying ability. A defensible decision identifies the claim the score is being used to support, examines relevant barriers, and adds evidence where the claim exceeds what one test establishes. How best to combine that evidence may remain uncertain in an individual case. What is clear is that comparability, consistent measurement, and fair interpretation are separate achievements that need to support one another.

choices.text: Their performance under the scoring rules matched, while broader ability remains a separate question.

questions.stem: How could a consistent test still raise a fairness concern?
questions.stem_ja: 一貫した結果を出すテストでも、なお公平性の懸念が生じうるのはなぜか。

choices.text: Its stable results might reduce the need to define the subject being assessed.

choices.text: Its common scoring rules might make results harder to compare across classrooms.
choices.text_ja: 共通の採点基準によって、教室間で結果を比べにくくなるかもしれないから。

questions.stem: Which revision best matches the passage's distinction between relevant and irrelevant language demands?

choices.text_ja: 課題を見直す前に、生徒の言語集団に応じて数学の点数を調整する。

choices.text: Remove difficult reading from a reading test so that language backgrounds affect results less.

choices.text: Use simpler unnecessary wording on a mathematics task while preserving its reasoning demand.
choices.text_ja: 数学の課題で、推論の負担は保ちつつ、不必要な言い回しをより簡単にする。

questions.stem: What makes an additional assessment particularly useful?

choices.text_ja: 同じ問題パターンを使い、点数どうしが一致しやすくなる場合。

choices.text: It addresses a specific uncertainty with relevant evidence whose own limits are examined.
choices.text_ja: 特定の不確かさに、関連する証拠で対応し、その証拠自体の限界も検討されている場合。

choices.text: It gives teachers more freedom to score work according to local expectations.
choices.text_ja: 教師が地域の期待に応じて作品を採点できる自由が増える場合。

questions.stem: Why does considering background require caution?
questions.stem_ja: 生徒の背景を考慮する際に慎重さが必要なのはなぜか。

passage.title: Why Antibiotic Stewardship Matters

paragraphs.text: In the fictional Northbridge health district, many patients recovered after receiving antibiotics, yet laboratory reports showed an increasing proportion of tested bacteria resisting some commonly used drugs. The two observations seemed contradictory to residents who judged treatment by whether someone felt better afterward. Clinicians recognized that the observations concerned different questions. A patient's improvement did not establish that every prescription had been necessary, while a regional resistance pattern did not show that antibiotics had stopped helping patients. The district began examining the decisions behind prescribing instead of treating either observation as a complete verdict on the medicines.

Antibiotics are valuable against susceptible bacterial infections. They do not treat viruses, and similar symptoms can have different causes. Improvement after a prescription therefore needs careful interpretation: some illnesses would have improved without that drug. At the same time, delaying appropriate treatment for a serious bacterial infection can be dangerous. The district's clinicians were not choosing between believing in antibiotics and rejecting them. They needed to decide when the likely benefits justified use, then select suitable treatment in light of the patient's condition and the information available.

The regional concern involved selection among bacteria. When an antibiotic affects susceptible bacteria, those able to resist it may survive and multiply. Resistant bacteria can then spread, affecting people beyond the original patient. Use that provides little clinical benefit can still contribute to this pressure. Resistance is a property of the bacteria, not a sign that a patient's body has become accustomed to medicine. The consequences are also distributed unevenly across time: a prescription's hoped-for benefit is immediate and visible, while its contribution to a wider problem is harder to identify in a single encounter.

Reviewing records, Northbridge's team discovered that clinics described similar situations in different ways. Some records clearly stated the suspected infection and the reason for treatment; others contained a drug name with little explanation. This made comparisons difficult. The district introduced shared guidance based on clinical evidence, asked clinicians to document their reasons, and improved access to local laboratory information. The guidance still allowed decisions appropriate to individual patients. Uniform recording was meant to make variation understandable, not to require identical treatment whenever two people reported a similar symptom.

Another change concerned review. A decision made before test results were available could be reconsidered when new evidence arrived. If treatment was necessary, clinicians could check whether the chosen drug remained appropriate; if the evidence did not support it, they could revise the plan. Patients received explanations of the decision and of the follow-up arrangements. This mattered because an encounter ending without an antibiotic could otherwise feel like an encounter ending without care. Assessment, explanation, and monitoring remained clinical work even when they did not produce a prescription.

The district then faced a measurement problem. A falling prescription count might reflect improved practice, but it might also reflect fewer infections, different patients, or missed treatment. The team therefore examined reasons for prescribing alongside patient outcomes and resistance information. It also considered changes in which samples laboratories tested, since an increase among tested samples might not represent the same increase across the whole population. These checks did not erase the resistance concern. They helped prevent a convenient total from becoming the goal regardless of what happened to patients.

Northbridge's experience illustrates why stewardship means improving antibiotic use rather than simply reducing it. Individual care and population protection can support one another when unnecessary exposure is avoided and effective treatment is preserved. Difficult cases still involve uncertainty, especially before a diagnosis is clear. Shared evidence, documented reasoning, and timely review help make those decisions accountable without pretending that a common rule removes every judgment. The district could not promise that its policy would eliminate resistance. It could define success more responsibly: appropriate treatment now, assessed together with the effort to preserve useful treatment for patients who will need it later.

choices.text_ja: 似たような症状は、一般に、選ばれた薬に耐性のある感染症を示していたから。

choices.text: It can shift the samples being tested toward resistant infections, which then increases resistance in the community.

choices.text: It can favor resistant bacteria that survive and later spread.

choices.text: It can make a later prescription less effective because the original patient's body adapts to the drug.
choices.text_ja: もとの患者の体が薬に適応するため、後の処方の効き目が弱くなる。

questions.stem: What was the purpose of combining documented reasons with later review?
questions.stem_ja: 判断の理由を記録することと、後の見直しとを組み合わせた目的は何か。

choices.text: To transfer responsibility for individual decisions from clinicians to the shared guidance.

choices.text: To treat similar symptoms consistently before considering differences between patients.

choices.text: To make initial prescriptions comparable enough that treatment could continue unchanged.
choices.text_ja: 最初の処方を十分に比較可能にし、治療を変更せずに続けられるようにするため。

choices.text: To make decisions understandable and revise them when additional evidence became available.
choices.text_ja: 判断を理解できるものにし、新たな証拠が得られたときにそれを修正するため。

questions.stem: Which finding would make a lower prescription total ambiguous as evidence of success?
questions.stem_ja: 処方件数の合計が減ったことを成功の証拠とみなすのを曖昧にするのは、どの発見か。

choices.text: Patients received clearer information about follow-up arrangements.
choices.text_ja: 患者が経過観察の段取りについて、よりわかりやすい説明を受けた。

choices.text_ja: 比較期間中、保健区で治療した感染症の患者が少なかった。

choices.text_ja: 疑われる感染症と治療の理由を説明している記録が増えた。

passage.title: The Complicated History of Rewilding

paragraphs.text: An old landscape photograph can become a powerful object at a restoration ceremony. Imagine one displayed beside a newly restored area: a river curves through open ground, and a few trees stand along its banks. The photograph invites viewers to compare past and present. It does not tell them why that particular date should define the future. An earlier image might show denser woodland, while a later one might show fields. Rewilding, which seeks to restore ecological processes and relationships, must address this difficulty even when everyone agrees that the current landscape has been damaged.

From an ecologist's viewpoint, the photograph is a source of clues rather than a complete target. It shows some visible features but leaves out many organisms and interactions. A healthy ecosystem involves processes such as reproduction, movement, and the cycling of nutrients, not just a familiar appearance. Restoring those processes may require knowledge of past conditions, yet choosing one moment can hide the fact that landscapes have long been changing. A reference condition can guide a project without becoming a demand to reproduce every detail of a single historical picture.

A resident may read the same photograph differently. The open ground could recall grazing animals, seasonal work, or a route used between settlements. Human activity may have helped maintain the landscape that viewers now call natural. This does not prove that every traditional practice benefited every species. It does show why removing people from the story can produce a mistaken account of how a place developed. Local knowledge can identify past uses and changes that a photograph cannot explain, although memories also vary and need to be considered alongside other evidence.

For an administrator, choosing a target creates another set of responsibilities. A project needs a basis for allocating funds, explaining restrictions, and deciding whether progress has occurred. A recognizable historical image offers a simple public goal. A process-based goal, such as restoring movement between habitats, may be less immediately visible but more relevant to ecological recovery. The difficulty is not resolved by selecting whichever goal is easiest to count. Measures should correspond to the purpose of the project, while the people affected need to understand how that purpose will change their use of the area.

These viewpoints can overlap without becoming identical. In a hypothetical valley, residents might support restoring a river connection while disagreeing about ending grazing on nearby land. An ecologist might expect different ecological outcomes from the two actions, and an administrator might need separate agreements for each. Treating the entire plan as a choice between supporting nature and opposing it would conceal those distinctions. Breaking the plan into actions, expected effects, and affected interests allows disagreement to become more specific. It also helps reveal proposals that serve several goals and proposals that involve a real tradeoff.

The future further complicates the choice of a past reference. Conditions that once supported a particular arrangement may change, including climate and the surrounding pattern of land use. A project designed to preserve an exact historical appearance could therefore demand continuing intervention even while being described as a return to self-sustaining nature. Allowing ecological processes to respond to change may produce a landscape unlike the chosen photograph. That possibility does not remove the need for goals or monitoring. It requires distinguishing an acceptable change from a failure to restore the processes the project intended to support.

The photograph remains useful at the end of this discussion, but its role has changed. It documents one view of a place at one time; it does not independently select the most appropriate future. Scientific evidence can clarify ecological consequences, local history can reveal human relationships, and public decisions must address competing priorities. The observation that a landscape once looked a certain way is separate from the judgment that it should look that way again. Rewilding becomes more coherent when that judgment is made openly and when recovery is understood as a living process rather than a frozen scene.
