choices.text: It establishes past conditions accurately enough that future changes become difficult to measure.
choices.text_ja: 過去の状態をあまりに正確に示すため、将来の変化を測るのが難しくなる。

choices.text: It makes earlier landscapes less reliable sources than memories of recent land use.
choices.text_ja: 以前の景観が、最近の土地利用についての記憶よりも信頼できない資料になってしまう。

choices.text: It records one appearance without establishing which processes or historical moment should guide recovery.
choices.text_ja: 一つの見た目を記録しているだけで、どのプロセスや歴史上の時点が回復の指針となるべきかは示さない。

questions.stem: How can local history complement ecological evidence?
questions.stem_ja: 地元の歴史は、生態学的な証拠をどのように補いうるか。

choices.text: It can replace the need to investigate processes absent from the photograph.
choices.text_ja: 写真に写っていないプロセスを調べる必要をなくすことができる。

choices.text: It can identify human activities that helped shape features otherwise interpreted as purely natural.
choices.text_ja: 本来なら純粋に自然のものと解釈される特徴を形づくるのに役立った人間の活動を特定できる。

choices.text: It can show which traditional activities benefited every species in the area.
choices.text_ja: どの伝統的な活動がその地域のあらゆる生物種に役立ったかを示すことができる。

choices.text: It can provide a preferred date that ecological evidence is unable to question.
choices.text_ja: 生態学的な証拠が疑問を差し挟めないような、望ましい時点を示すことができる。

questions.stem: Which approach would best clarify disagreement about the hypothetical valley?
questions.stem_ja: 仮想の谷をめぐる意見の対立を明確にするのに、最も適した方法はどれか。

choices.text: Use the historical photograph to decide which proposed actions count as natural.
choices.text_ja: 歴史的な写真を使って、提案された措置のうちどれが自然なものかを決める。

choices.text: Choose the action with the most visible result so residents can judge progress.
choices.text_ja: 住民が進展を判断できるよう、最も目に見える結果をもたらす措置を選ぶ。

choices.text: Compare each action's expected effects and affected interests separately.
choices.text_ja: 各措置について、予想される効果と影響を受ける利害を別々に比較する。

choices.text: Ask residents to approve the whole plan before discussing particular restrictions.
choices.text_ja: 個々の制限について話し合う前に、計画全体を承認するよう住民に求める。

questions.stem: Why might a successful process-based project come to look unlike its historical reference?
questions.stem_ja: プロセスに基づく計画が成功した場合でも、その景観が歴史的な基準とは似ていないものになりうるのはなぜか。

choices.text: Historical images usually show temporary damage rather than healthy conditions.
choices.text_ja: 歴史的な写真は、たいてい健全な状態ではなく一時的な損傷を写しているから。

choices.text: Restoring a reference condition requires removing the local practices that produced it.
choices.text_ja: 基準となる状態を回復させるには、その状態を生み出した地元の営みを取り除く必要があるから。

choices.text: Process goals are too difficult to monitor against any meaningful standard.
choices.text_ja: プロセスの目標は、意味のある基準に照らして監視するのが難しすぎるから。

choices.text: Functioning ecological processes can respond to conditions that differ from the past.
choices.text_ja: 正常に働く生態系のプロセスは、過去とは異なる条件に応じて変わりうるから。

questions.stem: What distinction does the conclusion ask readers to preserve?
questions.stem_ja: 結論で筆者が読者に保つよう求めている区別はどれか。

choices.text: Evidence of a past landscape differs from a judgment that it should be recreated.
choices.text_ja: 過去の景観の証拠と、それを再現すべきだという判断とは異なる。

choices.text: A project can prioritize ecological processes once human interests have been excluded.
choices.text_ja: 人間の利害が除外されれば、計画は生態系のプロセスを優先できる。

choices.text: Scientific evidence determines goals, whereas local history determines how to fund them.
choices.text_ja: 科学的な証拠が目標を決め、地元の歴史がその資金の調達方法を決める。

choices.text: Changing conditions make historical evidence less useful than public preferences.
choices.text_ja: 条件が変化するため、歴史的な証拠は人々の好みほど役に立たない。

passage.title: What Makes a Promise Binding?

paragraphs.text: A borrowed van waits outside a house on Saturday morning. In this hypothetical situation, its owner has promised to help a friend move, then receives an invitation to a more enjoyable event. Keeping the promise now carries a personal cost. The invitation makes a familiar question concrete: why should the earlier commitment have authority over a later preference? Saying that promises should be kept identifies a principle, but does not yet explain its force. Two possible explanations focus on different things: the benefits of reliable cooperation and the claim created when another person is given an assurance.

The first explanation begins with what promising enables people to do together. Friends can arrange a move, workers can coordinate tasks, and strangers can exchange goods because they expect commitments to matter. Even someone who occasionally loses an attractive opportunity may benefit from living among reliable partners. In the van example, keeping the promise supports a practice from which both friends gain over time. This explanation need not say that every kept promise brings an immediate reward. Its strength lies in connecting individual inconvenience to the broader advantages of being able to plan with others.

A second explanation gives special weight to the person who received the promise. The friend may have declined other help and arranged the day around the van. By giving an assurance, the owner helped create that reliance. On this view, the obligation is not exhausted by asking whether keeping promises is generally useful. The friend has a particular claim that deserves an answer. Even if abandoning the move would produce more total enjoyment, the owner's new preference does not erase the assurance. Asking the friend to release the commitment recognizes that the recipient has a role in deciding what happens next.

The difference becomes clearer in an emergency. Suppose that, before departure, the van is urgently needed to take someone away from immediate danger, and no suitable alternative is available. A benefits-based account can explain using the van for that purpose by comparing the consequences. An account centered on the friend's claim can also permit the change, while insisting that an urgent competing obligation differs from a convenient new invitation. Neither approach needs to treat the original promise as meaningless. Explaining the interruption, arranging substitute help when possible, and acknowledging the inconvenience may remain appropriate.

Now change one feature of the example. Suppose the emergency can be handled equally well by another available vehicle, leaving the promised van free. The mere presence of an emergency no longer gives the same reason to abandon the move. This comparison matters because labels such as 'urgent' do not settle the relevant facts. The seriousness of the need, the available alternatives, and the cost of delaying action affect the justification. A reasonable exception is connected to those conditions, rather than to whichever description makes a preferred choice sound more important.

The two explanations can nevertheless disagree in harder cases. An action might produce slightly better overall results while placing a serious, unchosen burden on the recipient of a promise. A calculation focused on benefits and an account focused on that person's claim may weigh the situation differently. There is no need to hide this disagreement by pretending that one example settles every philosophical question. The comparison instead identifies shared constraints: a changed preference is different from a serious competing need, reliance matters to the assessment, and an exception calls for reasons that others can examine.

The van outside the house therefore represents more than a choice between pleasure and duty. A promise changes the basis on which people organize their actions, and abandoning it requires more explanation than simply choosing differently before it was made. Exceptional circumstances can justify a departure without turning the original assurance into an empty statement. The precise source and strength of the obligation remain open to argument. What the examples establish is narrower: evaluating a broken promise requires attention to its recipient, the reasons for departure, and the alternatives actually available.

questions.stem: How do the two explanations differ?
questions.stem_ja: 二つの説明はどのように異なるか。

choices.text: One requires immediate rewards; the other allows benefits to emerge over time.
choices.text_ja: 一方はすぐに見返りがあることを求め、もう一方は利益が時間をかけて生じることを認める。

choices.text: One emphasizes benefits of reliable cooperation; the other emphasizes a particular recipient's claim.
choices.text_ja: 一方は信頼できる協力の利益を重視し、もう一方は約束を受けた特定の人の請求権を重視する。

choices.text: One concerns promises between friends; the other applies mainly to exchanges between strangers.
choices.text_ja: 一方は友人どうしの約束に関するもので、もう一方は主に見知らぬ者どうしのやり取りに当てはまる。

choices.text: One permits inconvenience; the other treats inconvenience as evidence that a promise should end.
choices.text_ja: 一方は不便を許容し、もう一方は不便を約束をやめるべき根拠とみなす。

questions.stem: Why would asking the friend for release from the promise be significant?
questions.stem_ja: 友人に約束を取り消してもらえるよう頼むことが重要なのはなぜか。

choices.text: It would recognize the friend's standing in deciding how the commitment is changed.
choices.text_ja: 約束をどう変えるかを決めるうえで、友人にも立場があることを認めることになるから。

choices.text: It would establish that attending the invitation produces the best overall outcome.
choices.text_ja: 誘いに応じる方が全体として最良の結果をもたらすことが確定するから。

choices.text: It would remove the relevance of the friend's earlier reliance on the van.
choices.text_ja: 友人が以前からバンを当てにしていたことが問題でなくなるから。

choices.text: It would show that the original assurance was too uncertain to create a claim.
choices.text_ja: もとの保証があいまいすぎて請求権を生まなかったことが示されるから。

questions.stem: Why does the availability of another vehicle change the emergency example?
questions.stem_ja: ほかに使える車があることで、緊急事態の例はなぜ変わるのか。

choices.text: It gives the van's owner greater authority to decide whether the friend relied on the promise.
choices.text_ja: 友人が約束を当てにしていたかどうかを判断する権限が、バンの持ち主により多く与えられるから。

choices.text: It turns an urgent competing obligation into a question about long-term cooperation alone.
choices.text_ja: 差し迫った別の義務が、長期的な協力だけに関わる問題に変わるから。

choices.text: It reduces the friend's inconvenience enough to make personal preference decisive.
choices.text_ja: 友人の不便が十分に小さくなり、個人的な好みが決め手になるから。

choices.text: It weakens the reason for diverting this van from its promised use.
choices.text_ja: このバンを約束した用途からほかに回す理由が弱まるから。

questions.stem: What can remain appropriate even when breaking the promise is justified?
questions.stem_ja: 約束を破ることが正当化される場合でも、依然として適切でありうるのは何か。

choices.text: Showing that the emergency will bring the owner a long-term benefit.
choices.text_ja: その緊急事態が持ち主に長期的な利益をもたらすと示すこと。

choices.text: Seeking agreement that future promises should have weaker force in similar situations.
choices.text_ja: 同じような状況では、今後の約束の拘束力を弱めることに同意を求めること。

choices.text: Explaining the change and addressing the burden imposed on the friend where possible.
choices.text_ja: 変更について説明し、可能な範囲で友人に生じた負担に対処すること。

choices.text: Treating the friend's inconvenience as irrelevant once the emergency has been identified.
choices.text_ja: 緊急事態だと分かった時点で、友人の不便を考慮の外に置くこと。

questions.stem: Which question is most useful when assessing a claimed exception?
questions.stem_ja: 例外だという主張を評価する際に、最も役立つ問いはどれか。

choices.text: Could the serious competing need have been met without abandoning the promise?
choices.text_ja: その深刻な別の必要は、約束を破らずに満たすことができたか。

choices.text: Would the owner have preferred the alternative activity before making the promise?
choices.text_ja: 持ち主は約束をする前から、もう一方の活動の方を好んでいたか。

choices.text: Has the promise already produced enough cooperative benefit to offset its recipient's loss?
choices.text_ja: その約束はすでに、約束を受けた人の損失を埋め合わせるだけの協力の利益を生んでいるか。

choices.text: Do both parties accept the same general philosophical account of promising?
choices.text_ja: 双方が、約束について同じ一般的な哲学的説明を受け入れているか。

passage.title: The Unequal Benefits of Bike Lanes

paragraphs.text: A bicycle counter beside the main library in the fictional city of Eastmere recorded busy morning traffic. A counter beside a newly built lane in an outer district recorded much less. Both lanes met the city's design requirements, and both had been announced as improvements in access. The contrast prompted officials to ask why similar lengths of new infrastructure produced different use. One answer was that residents simply had different preferences. A closer examination showed that a cycling journey depended on several connected conditions, some of which the new lanes had not changed.

A protected lane gives riders space separated from some motor traffic and can reduce particular conflicts when its connections and crossings are well designed. That is a meaningful improvement along the section where it exists. A journey, however, begins before that section and continues after it. The library lane connected nearby housing to shops, offices, and an existing route. The outer lane ended at a wide road with a difficult crossing. Residents there could use the new section yet still face a gap on the way to a common destination. Counting completed lane length treated these two improvements as more alike than their users experienced them.

Distance created another condition. Many residents near the library had destinations within a practical cycling distance. In the outer district, some jobs were much farther away. A good local lane could still be useful for school or shopping trips without replacing those longer commutes. Household circumstances also differed. Carrying equipment, accompanying children, or having a disability could affect whether a particular route and bicycle were suitable. These observations did not imply that the outer district had no demand. They showed why a count of current cyclists could not fully describe either the barriers or the trips residents wanted to make.

The transport office considered two uses for its next budget. Extending the busy central route could serve many existing riders and relieve a crowded section. Completing connections in the outer district might enable trips that were currently difficult, even if early counts remained lower. The first proposal had stronger evidence of immediate use. The second addressed a barrier that might partly explain low use. Treating present numbers as the complete measure of need would favor places where a useful network already existed, while treating every underused lane as hidden demand would be equally unjustified.

To compare the proposals, Eastmere separated several measures. Counts showed observed use at particular points and times. Surveys and route discussions helped identify destinations and obstacles, though stated intentions did not guarantee future cycling. Accessibility analysis examined whether residents could reach useful places through a connected route. The city also asked who would gain from each proposal, rather than assuming that a larger total benefit meant a wider distribution. These measures answered related questions without being interchangeable. A project could attract many trips while leaving certain residents with little improvement in their available choices.

In a small trial, the city improved a connection at the end of the outer lane and recorded journeys before and after the change. It compared similar periods and noted weather differences, rather than attributing every increase to the new connection. Residents' comments helped distinguish new cycling journeys from trips merely shifted from another nearby route. The trial provided more relevant evidence than the lane's original low count alone. It did not settle whether the full outer network deserved priority over the central extension, since cost, additional connections, and the distribution of benefits still had to be considered.

The two counters thus remained useful, but their disagreement no longer looked like a simple ranking of successful and unsuccessful districts. The busy route benefited from a network and nearby destinations; the quieter route exposed a missing link among several constraints. Fair allocation required the city to state whether it prioritized immediate use, expanded travel options, underserved residents, or some combination. Total lane length could document construction, and rider counts could document activity. Neither could independently decide how fairly the city had improved people's ability to travel.

questions.stem: What best explains why equal lane lengths could provide unequal practical access?
questions.stem_ja: 同じ長さのレーンが、実際の移動のしやすさに差をもたらしえた理由として最も適切なものはどれか。

choices.text: The library counter measured all city trips rather than cycling journeys.
choices.text_ja: 図書館のカウンターが、自転車での移動ではなく市内のすべての移動を計測していたから。

choices.text: The outer lane had lower design standards despite meeting the announced requirements.
choices.text_ja: 郊外のレーンは、発表された基準は満たしていたものの、設計の水準が低かったから。

choices.text: The outer lane served fewer destinations because residents preferred motor transport.
choices.text_ja: 住民が自動車での移動を好んだため、郊外のレーンが結ぶ目的地が少なかったから。

choices.text: The lanes connected differently to the rest of a journey and its destinations.
choices.text_ja: レーンが、移動の残りの部分や目的地と、それぞれ異なる形でつながっていたから。

questions.stem: Why should low current use not be treated as a complete measure of need?
questions.stem_ja: 現在の利用が少ないことを、必要性のすべてを測る尺度として扱うべきでないのはなぜか。

choices.text: It shows that short shopping trips should take priority over longer commutes.
choices.text_ja: 短い買い物の移動を、長い通勤より優先すべきことを示しているから。

choices.text: It indicates that surveys of intended cycling are more accurate than actual counts.
choices.text_ja: 自転車利用の意向を尋ねるアンケートのほうが、実際の計数より正確であることを示しているから。

choices.text: It may partly reflect barriers that prevent desired trips from being made.
choices.text_ja: 望んでいる移動を妨げている障壁を、部分的に反映しているかもしれないから。

choices.text: It demonstrates that connecting the outer district will create more trips than a central extension.
choices.text_ja: 郊外の地区を接続すれば、中心部の延長よりも多くの移動が生まれることを証明しているから。

questions.stem: What is the main difference between the two budget proposals?
questions.stem_ja: 二つの予算案の主な違いは何か。

choices.text: The central proposal addresses disabilities, whereas the outer proposal addresses commute distance.
choices.text_ja: 中心部の案は障害に対応し、郊外の案は通勤距離に対応する。

choices.text: The central proposal serves demonstrated use, whereas the outer proposal may remove a barrier to use.
choices.text_ja: 中心部の案は実証済みの利用に応え、郊外の案は利用を妨げる障壁を取り除くかもしれない。

choices.text: The central proposal has lower costs, whereas the outer proposal offers a wider distribution.
choices.text_ja: 中心部の案は費用が低く、郊外の案は恩恵がより広く行き渡る。

choices.text: The central proposal improves access, whereas the outer proposal primarily measures construction.
choices.text_ja: 中心部の案は移動のしやすさを改善し、郊外の案は主に建設の量を測る。

questions.stem: Why distinguish new cycling journeys from trips shifted from another route?
questions.stem_ja: 自転車での新たな移動と、別のルートから移ってきた移動とを区別するのはなぜか。

choices.text: The same counter increase can represent different changes in overall cycling activity.
choices.text_ja: カウンターの数が同じだけ増えても、それが表す自転車利用全体の変化は異なりうるから。

choices.text: Shifted journeys indicate that the improved connection did not help any residents.
choices.text_ja: 移ってきた移動は、改善された接続がどの住民の役にも立たなかったことを示すから。

choices.text: Shifted journeys are better evidence of future demand than new journeys.
choices.text_ja: 移ってきた移動のほうが、新たな移動よりも将来の需要を示す良い証拠になるから。

choices.text: New journeys can be assessed without considering weather or comparison periods.
choices.text_ja: 新たな移動は、天候や比較する時期を考慮せずに評価できるから。

questions.stem: What additional judgment is needed beyond a total count of beneficiaries?
questions.stem_ja: 恩恵を受ける人の総数に加えて、どのような判断が必要か。

choices.text: Whether a larger count can replace evidence about route connections.
choices.text_ja: 数が大きければ、ルートの接続に関する証拠の代わりになるかどうか。

choices.text: Whether the busiest route should become the standard for all district designs.
choices.text_ja: 最も混雑するルートを、すべての地区の設計の標準とすべきかどうか。

choices.text: Whether the project distribution matches the city's stated fairness priorities.
choices.text_ja: 事業による恩恵の配分が、市が明言した公平性の優先事項に合っているかどうか。

choices.text: Whether residents who do not currently cycle should be excluded from the comparison.
choices.text_ja: 現在自転車に乗っていない住民を、比較から除外すべきかどうか。

passage.title: The Discovery That Needed New Instruments

paragraphs.text: As measuring instruments have become more sensitive, phenomena once beyond observation have become available for investigation. This history can be explored through an imagined discovery, without assigning invented results to a real laboratory. Suppose a theory predicts a faint, regular signal. Earlier instruments produce records containing fluctuations, but no clearly identifiable pattern of the predicted kind. Supporters of the theory argue that the signal is hidden; critics argue that the records provide no confirmation. Both positions can contain something reasonable. The dispute turns partly on what the instruments were capable of distinguishing, not merely on which group found the theory more persuasive.

An instrument records a combination of the target effect and other influences. Some fluctuations may arise from its own operation; others may come from the surrounding environment. A signal smaller than these background variations can be difficult to separate from them. Calibration, which compares an instrument's response with suitable references, helps establish what its readings mean. It does not automatically remove every source of uncertainty. Before interpreting an absence of detection, investigators need to know the range of signals the equipment could reliably reveal under the conditions in which it was used.

The critic can therefore make a limited but important claim: the old record does not establish the predicted phenomenon. A stronger claim, that the phenomenon does not exist, requires more. If a device should have detected a signal of the predicted size and no signal appeared, the result would count against that prediction. If the expected signal lay below the device's effective capability, the same absence would be less informative. Explaining a missing result through limited sensitivity is legitimate when that limitation is independently supported, rather than invented whenever a favored theory fails.

The supporter faces a parallel limit. A theory can guide the search by predicting a signal's size, timing, or pattern, but a prediction is not a detection. In the imagined investigation, these predictions help engineers choose what to improve. They reduce one source of background variation and construct a detector with a response better suited to the expected pattern. The new records contain a candidate signal. This is progress, although the instrument's improvement alone does not settle the interpretation. A new device can introduce unfamiliar disturbances as well as reveal effects previously hidden.

Investigators must now ask whether the candidate behaves as expected and whether alternative explanations survive. They can change conditions that the theory says should affect the signal, check periods when it should be absent, and compare results from independently operated equipment. Repeating the same reading on one instrument is useful but may repeat the same unnoticed error. Agreement across approaches with different weaknesses can provide stronger support. The goal is not to demand a magical measurement free of uncertainty. It is to show that the evidence favors the proposed phenomenon after plausible sources of misleading patterns have been examined.

Once the signal is well supported, the improved equipment may change the research question. Investigators can move from asking whether the effect is detectable to asking how it varies. The theory may then need refinement if the measured variation differs from its predictions. Thus technology does more than provide a final stamp of approval for an idea already complete. It creates opportunities for observations that can reshape the idea. Equally, those technical improvements were partly directed by theoretical expectations about what might be worth detecting and which distinctions mattered.

The original disagreement can now be stated more precisely. The old instruments supplied neither convincing confirmation nor, if their sensitivity was inadequate, a decisive rejection. New instruments made a stronger test possible, while independent checks connected a candidate pattern to a defensible discovery. This account gives theory and measurement different but interacting roles. A prediction helps specify a search; a capable instrument makes relevant evidence obtainable; critical comparisons determine how much that evidence supports. Scientific progress depends on keeping those roles connected without treating any one of them as a substitute for the others.

questions.stem: When would failure to detect the signal count more strongly against the prediction?
questions.stem_ja: 信号が検出されなかったことが、予測に対してより強い反証となるのはどのような場合か。

choices.text: Supporters and critics agreed that the predicted pattern was worth seeking.
choices.text_ja: 支持者と批判者が、予測されたパターンは探す価値があるという点で一致していた場合。

choices.text: Equipment could reliably detect signals of the predicted size under those conditions.
choices.text_ja: その条件のもとで、装置が予測された大きさの信号を確実に検出できた場合。

choices.text: Several improvements to instrument design had already been guided by the theory.
choices.text_ja: 装置の設計に対するいくつかの改良が、すでにその理論にもとづいて行われていた場合。

choices.text: Calibration was complete, although substantial background variation remained.
choices.text_ja: 較正は完了していたが、かなりの背景の変動が残っていた場合。

questions.stem: What limit applies to the theory's supporters?
questions.stem_ja: 理論の支持者には、どのような限界が当てはまるか。

choices.text: They cannot treat a plausible prediction as evidence that the phenomenon has been observed.
choices.text_ja: もっともらしい予測を、その現象が観測されたことの証拠として扱うことはできない。

choices.text: They should prefer repeated old measurements to improvements designed around the theory.
choices.text_ja: 理論にもとづいて設計された改良よりも、古い測定の繰り返しを優先すべきである。

choices.text: They should avoid using predicted patterns to guide the design of a detector.
choices.text_ja: 予測されたパターンを検出器の設計の指針として使うことは避けるべきである。

choices.text: They must show that the old instrument produced no useful measurements of any kind.
choices.text_ja: 古い装置がどんな種類の有用な測定値も生み出さなかったことを示さなければならない。

questions.stem: Why is a candidate pattern from the improved device insufficient by itself?
questions.stem_ja: 改良された装置から得られた信号の候補が、それだけでは不十分なのはなぜか。

choices.text: Improved sensitivity makes comparison with theoretical expectations less reliable.
choices.text_ja: 感度が高まると、理論上の予想との比較の信頼性が下がるから。

choices.text: The original theory described a signal that should remain below every detector's capability.
choices.text_ja: もとの理論は、どの検出器の能力も下回るはずの信号を述べていたから。

choices.text: The new equipment may produce disturbances that resemble the proposed signal.
choices.text_ja: 新しい装置が、提案された信号に似た妨害を生み出すかもしれないから。

choices.text: Independent equipment would need identical weaknesses before its results could be compared.
choices.text_ja: 独立した装置の結果を比べるには、それらがまったく同じ弱点を持っている必要があるから。

questions.stem: Why can agreement across different approaches be more persuasive than repeated readings on one device?
questions.stem_ja: 異なる手法の間で結果が一致することが、一つの装置での繰り返し測定よりも説得力を持ちうるのはなぜか。

choices.text: One device cannot provide repeatable readings if its uncertainty is known.
choices.text_ja: 一つの装置は、不確かさが分かっている場合、再現可能な測定値を出せないから。

choices.text: It reduces the chance that the same unnoticed instrument problem explains every result.
choices.text_ja: 気づかれていない同じ装置の問題がすべての結果を説明してしまう可能性が低くなるから。

choices.text: Different approaches remove the need to test when the signal should be absent.
choices.text_ja: 異なる手法を用いれば、信号がないはずのときを検証する必要がなくなるから。

choices.text: Agreement across approaches establishes that every source of error has disappeared.
choices.text_ja: 手法の間で結果が一致すれば、あらゆる誤差の原因がなくなったことが立証されるから。

questions.stem: How can improved equipment affect a theory after an effect has been detected?
questions.stem_ja: 効果が検出された後、改良された装置は理論にどのような影響を与えうるか。

choices.text: It can make earlier questions about detection irrelevant to interpreting the evidence.
choices.text_ja: 検出に関する以前の問いを、証拠の解釈とは無関係なものにしうる。

choices.text: It can establish that the theory no longer requires predictions of variation.
choices.text_ja: その理論がもはや変化についての予測を必要としないことを立証しうる。

choices.text: It can transfer responsibility for explanation entirely to engineering design.
choices.text_ja: 説明の責任をすべて工学的な設計に移しうる。

choices.text: It can reveal patterns of variation that require the theory to be refined.
choices.text_ja: 理論の修正を必要とするような変化のパターンを明らかにしうる。

passage.title: Whose Story Does a Monument Tell?

paragraphs.text: When the fictional town of Bellhaven erected its harbor monument, the inscription praised the merchants who financed a new port. Generations later, the stone remained in the same square, but the town's discussion of the harbor had changed. Residents now asked whose work had made the expansion possible and whose neighborhood had been displaced. A proposal to replace the weathered explanation panel became a debate about the monument itself. The object had survived, while the questions addressed to it had multiplied. Repairing the stone was a practical task; deciding what the renewed display should say was a public judgment.

The original ceremony records explained why the merchants had been honored. Their supporters wanted to celebrate investment, employment, and the town's growing trade. The inscription reflected that purpose rather than offering a complete history of the harbor. It named donors but not the workers who built the docks or the households moved from the construction area. This did not make the inscription useless as evidence. It made it evidence of a particular commemorative choice: who the organizers considered worthy of public recognition when the monument was created.

Later records complicated the celebratory account. In Bellhaven's fictional archive, labor petitions described disputes over conditions, while property records documented the removal of homes. These sources did not establish that every worker opposed the port or that every displaced household had the same experience. They did establish that the original panel omitted important costs. The town's growing willingness to discuss those costs also reflected changing priorities. An earlier silence could no longer be treated as proof that the omitted people had accepted the story told on their behalf.

Different residents approached the stone through different memories. Some older residents associated the square with family gatherings and saw the monument as part of a familiar place. Descendants of displaced families associated it with a loss that public celebrations had ignored. Younger campaigners argued that continued display looked like continued approval of the original praise. Other younger residents preferred to keep the object visible so its selective message could be examined. The disagreement crossed generations as well as separating them; age alone did not predict a person's position.

The council considered removal, preservation without changes, and preservation with new interpretation. Moving the stone to a museum could change its role from civic honor to an object studied in context, though some residents feared losing a recognizable feature of the square. Leaving it untouched would preserve its original setting and message but would do little to address the omitted histories. New panels beside the stone could distinguish the original sponsors' purpose from later evidence and present several experiences. Such panels would require careful writing: placing incompatible claims side by side would not excuse the council from checking which claims the records supported.

The chosen plan kept the stone in the square and added a display explaining its creation, the harbor's benefits and costs, and the debate over its continued presence. Original wording remained visible and was clearly identified as the monument's own message. Accounts from residents were labeled as personal memories rather than presented as a single shared recollection. The council also preserved the records of its decision for later review. It did not announce that everyone had agreed or that adding information had removed the monument's emotional force. Some residents continued to prefer relocation.

Bellhaven had resolved what to do with the object for the time being, not whose relationship to it should become the town's final story. The revised display made more of the evidence accessible and clarified the difference between preserving an inscription and repeating its praise in the council's own voice. Whether this arrangement would remain acceptable was still uncertain. What had become clear was that a monument records an act of public selection as well as an event in the past. Preserving that record responsibly required room to question the selection, not merely to maintain the stone.

questions.stem: What does the original inscription most directly provide evidence about?
questions.stem_ja: もとの碑文が最も直接的に証拠となるのは何についてか。

choices.text: The organizers' choice of whom to honor at the time of construction.

choices.text: The relative economic contribution of every group involved in the harbor expansion.
choices.text_ja: 港の拡張に関わったすべての集団の、経済的貢献の相対的な大きさ。

choices.text: The extent to which displaced households accepted the port's benefits.
choices.text_ja: 立ち退かされた世帯が、港の利益をどの程度受け入れていたか。

choices.text: The harbor's net benefit after its financial and social costs were combined.
choices.text_ja: 経済的・社会的な代償を差し引いた後の、港の正味の利益。

questions.stem: What conclusion is supported by the petitions and property records?
questions.stem_ja: 請願書と不動産記録によって裏づけられる結論はどれか。

choices.text: The original display left out costs that deserve inclusion in the historical account.
choices.text_ja: もとの展示は、歴史の説明に含めるべき代償を省いていた。

choices.text: The later council had stronger economic reasons for keeping the monument than its founders.
choices.text_ja: 後の議会には、創設者たちよりも記念碑を残す強い経済的理由があった。

choices.text: The omission resulted from inaccurate records rather than the ceremony's purpose.
choices.text_ja: 省略が生じたのは、式典の目的のためではなく、記録が不正確だったためである。

choices.text: The port was opposed by most workers and all displaced residents.
choices.text_ja: 港には、大半の労働者と立ち退かされたすべての住民が反対していた。

questions.stem: Why does the passage describe disagreement among younger residents?
questions.stem_ja: 本文で、若い住民の間の意見の対立が述べられているのはなぜか。

choices.text: To suggest that relocation could satisfy the conflicting interpretations equally.
choices.text_ja: 移設によって、対立する解釈を等しく満足させられることを示唆するため。

choices.text: To show that a person's generation does not fully explain their view of the monument.
choices.text_ja: 人の世代だけでは、その人の記念碑に対する見方を十分に説明できないことを示すため。

choices.text: To establish that personal memories mattered more than documentary records in the debate.
choices.text_ja: 論争においては、文書記録よりも個人の記憶のほうが重要だったと立証するため。

choices.text: To show that younger residents knew less about the archive than older residents.
choices.text_ja: 若い住民は、年配の住民よりも公文書館について知らなかったことを示すため。

questions.stem: What responsibility remains when several interpretations are displayed?
questions.stem_ja: 複数の解釈を展示する場合に、なお残る責任は何か。

choices.text: Remove original wording that conflicts with later personal memories.
choices.text_ja: 後の個人の記憶と食い違うもとの文言を取り除くこと。

choices.text: Treat each personal memory as equally representative of the entire town.
choices.text_ja: 個人の記憶の一つ一つを、町全体を等しく代表するものとして扱うこと。

choices.text: Select the interpretation that attracts the largest number of visitors.
choices.text_ja: 最も多くの来訪者を引きつける解釈を選ぶこと。

choices.text: Check factual claims and clarify which statements are original praise or individual recollection.
choices.text_ja: 事実に関する主張を確かめ、どの記述がもとの賛辞で、どれが個人の回想なのかを明確にすること。

questions.stem: What did the chosen plan accomplish without resolving every disagreement?
questions.stem_ja: 選ばれた案は、すべての対立を解消しないまま、何を成し遂げたか。

choices.text: It established a shared account of the harbor that later councils could maintain unchanged.
choices.text_ja: 後の議会が変更せずに維持できる、港についての共通の説明を確立した。

choices.text: It separated historical evidence from emotional responses by removing the latter from the display.
choices.text_ja: 感情的な反応を展示から取り除くことで、歴史的証拠とそれとを切り離した。

choices.text: It exposed the commemorative choice to scrutiny without claiming that everyone endorsed preservation.
choices.text_ja: 全員が保存を支持したと主張することなく、記念の選択を検証の対象にした。

choices.text: It converted the square's monument into an exhibit removed from civic life.
choices.text_ja: 広場の記念碑を、町の暮らしから切り離された展示物に変えた。

passage.title: The Surprising Limits of Multitasking

paragraphs.text: As messages, shared documents, and online meetings have become easier to combine on one screen, visible activity has become an uncertain guide to completed work. Imagine someone reaching the end of an afternoon with many replies sent but a short report still unfinished. The person has been busy throughout, repeatedly moving between the report and incoming messages. It is tempting to explain the delay by counting only the minutes spent replying. Working backward from the unfinished report reveals another possible cost: each return may require recovering a line of thought and reestablishing what to do next.

Activities placed together are not necessarily demanding in the same way. Waiting for a file to download while writing a paragraph does not require continuous attention to both processes. Folding familiar items while having an undemanding conversation may also differ from composing an argument while answering detailed questions. The relevant distinction is the attention and control required at a particular moment, rather than whether two activity labels appear on a schedule. A combination can become harder if one task unexpectedly changes, even when it was manageable during its more routine phase.

Switching between demanding tasks requires adjusting goals and the rules currently guiding action. On returning to the report, the writer may need to recall the intended conclusion, locate supporting material, and distinguish the current sentence from an abandoned version. Thoughts from the intervening task can compete with that reconstruction. These costs need not involve a long conscious pause. Small disruptions repeated frequently can affect total completion time and errors. Feeling comfortable with a sequence of switches is therefore different from demonstrating that the sequence produces the same results as work organized another way.

In the imagined afternoon, notifications repeatedly determine when the writer changes tasks. One alternative would be to handle nonurgent messages in groups between periods of report writing. This could reduce the number of interruptions and make the transitions more deliberate. It would not make every message less important or every delay acceptable. A role requiring rapid responses has a different set of demands from one in which most messages can wait. The comparison needs to include both the report and the communication task; improving one outcome while overlooking failures in the other would give an incomplete account of efficiency.

Practice can change the balance. Familiar operations may require less conscious control, leaving more attention available for another activity. Preparation can also make a planned transition easier: a brief note identifying the next step may reduce the effort of resuming work. Neither observation implies that practice removes every switching cost. A routine task can become unfamiliar when a problem appears, and two well-practiced tasks may still compete for attention. It is more useful to ask which parts have become automatic and under what conditions than to label a person generally good or bad at multitasking.

Evaluating a proposed improvement therefore requires more than asking whether the afternoon felt calmer. In a hypothetical comparison, the writer could record completed work, mistakes requiring correction, and response delays under different arrangements. Similar task difficulty and communication demand would make the comparison more informative. A quieter day cannot by itself establish the benefit of grouped messages if it also contained a much easier report. Even a useful personal comparison would not automatically determine the best arrangement for someone whose responsibilities or tasks differ.

The unfinished report at the beginning is consistent with switching costs, but does not prove that they caused the entire delay. The explanation becomes stronger when alternatives are compared and other differences are considered. The practical implication is not a ban on all overlapping activity. It is to distinguish work that can proceed with little active control from combinations that repeatedly compete for it, and to judge arrangements by their actual outcomes. More visible motion among tasks can coexist with less progress through them; whether it does depends on what the tasks demand and how the transitions are managed.

questions.stem: Why might counting reply-writing minutes underestimate the effect of messages on report completion?
questions.stem_ja: 返信を書くのにかかった時間を数えるだけでは、メッセージが報告書の完成に与えた影響を過小評価しかねないのはなぜか。

choices.text: Messages generally require more attention than writing a report.
choices.text_ja: 一般に、メッセージは報告書を書くことよりも多くの注意を必要とするから。

choices.text: Returning to the report can require additional effort to recover goals and context.
choices.text_ja: 報告書に戻る際に、目標や文脈を取り戻すための余分な労力が必要になりうるから。

choices.text: Reply-writing time mainly measures the difficulty of the communication task.

choices.text: The report may include material obtained from the replies.
choices.text_ja: 報告書には、返信から得た内容が含まれているかもしれないから。

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes the file-download example from composing while answering detailed questions?
questions.stem_ja: ファイルのダウンロードの例と、細かい質問に答えながら文章を組み立てることを最も明確に区別する特徴はどれか。

choices.text: Both activities contribute to a single product, so their goals need less adjustment.
choices.text_ja: 両方の活動が一つの成果物に役立つので、目標の調整があまり必要ないこと。

choices.text: A download can continue while active attention remains on composing the paragraph.
choices.text_ja: 段落を書くことに積極的な注意を向けたままでも、ダウンロードは進み続けられること。

choices.text: The download's completion provides a planned transition, unlike the timing of a detailed question.

choices.text: Writing can be resumed from visible text, making its interruptions less costly than spoken questions.
choices.text_ja: 書く作業は目に見える文章から再開できるので、その中断は口頭の質問よりもコストが小さいこと。

questions.stem: What must be included when evaluating grouped message handling?
questions.stem_ja: メッセージをまとめて処理するやり方を評価する際に、含めなければならないことは何か。

choices.text: Whether the writer prefers report writing to answering questions.
choices.text_ja: 書き手が、質問に答えるよりも報告書を書くほうを好むかどうか。

choices.text: Whether it reduces the number of messages arriving during the afternoon.
choices.text_ja: 午後のあいだに届くメッセージの数が減るかどうか。

choices.text: Whether the report improves even if response requirements are missed.
choices.text_ja: 返信に求められることが果たされなくても、報告書が改善するかどうか。

choices.text: Whether both writing outcomes and necessary communication demands are met.
choices.text_ja: 文章を書く作業の成果と、必要なやりとりの要求の両方が満たされているかどうか。

questions.stem: What does practice permit an evaluator to conclude?
questions.stem_ja: 練習について、評価する人はどのような結論を下すことができるか。

choices.text: Some operations may demand less control, but the effect depends on the task and conditions.
choices.text_ja: 一部の操作に必要な制御は少なくなるかもしれないが、その効果は作業や条件によって変わる。

choices.text: A familiar task no longer needs monitoring when unexpected problems arise.
choices.text_ja: 慣れた作業は、予期しない問題が起きても、もはや注意を払う必要がない。

choices.text: Planned transitions can replace the need to examine competition between tasks.
choices.text_ja: 計画的な切り替えをすれば、作業どうしの注意の奪い合いを検討する必要はなくなる。

choices.text: A person successful with one task combination can be classified as an effective multitasker.
choices.text_ja: ある作業の組み合わせをうまくこなせる人は、マルチタスクが得意な人に分類できる。

questions.stem: Which comparison would provide stronger evidence for a benefit from grouped messages?
questions.stem_ja: メッセージをまとめて処理することの効果について、より強い証拠となる比較はどれか。

choices.text: Two workers' completion times without considering their different responsibilities.
choices.text_ja: 二人の働き手の作業完了時間を、それぞれの責任の違いを考慮せずに比べること。

choices.text: Reports of feeling calmer compared with the number of messages received.
choices.text_ja: 落ち着いたと感じたという報告を、受け取ったメッセージの数と比べること。

choices.text: Similar work demands assessed through completion, errors, and response delays under both arrangements.
choices.text_ja: 同程度の仕事の負担のもとで、両方のやり方について、完了、ミス、返信の遅れを評価すること。

choices.text: A difficult interrupted day compared with an easier uninterrupted afternoon.
choices.text_ja: 中断の多い難しい一日を、中断のない簡単な午後と比べること。

passage.title: A Seed Bank Facing Climate Change

paragraphs.text: Would a seed collected in a dry region mature early enough for farms with a short growing season? That was the question a farmer brought to the fictional Alder Seed Bank. The facility held many crop varieties and detailed records of where samples had been collected. The farmer wanted more than a list of origins. A recent change in local rainfall had made the timing of harvest increasingly important, and a variety that survived dry conditions but matured too late might offer little practical help. The inquiry exposed a gap between preserving possible resources and knowing which would work in a particular field.

The collection records were a valuable starting point. They identified samples, collection locations, and observations made when the material entered the bank. Such information could help researchers choose candidates rather than testing the entire collection at once. However, a place name summarized only part of a plant's history. Conditions within a dry region could vary, and the plants might have been grown with practices not recorded in the brief description. The label suggested questions worth asking; it did not answer how the sample would perform under the farmer's soil, planting date, and management.

Adaptation also involved more than surviving a lack of water. The length of the growing period, the timing of dry conditions, and other local pressures could affect usefulness. A variety might avoid a late dry period by maturing earlier, while another might continue growing through it but require a longer season. Both could be described loosely as useful under dryness, yet they would suit different circumstances. The bank's staff therefore asked the farmer to specify the problem: reaching harvest before a particular period of risk, maintaining yield with limited water, or some combination of goals.

They organized a fictional trial with several local farms. Each farm grew a small set of candidate varieties alongside its usual variety, recording planting dates, development, harvest timing, and yield. The comparison included repeated plots where practical, and staff noted management differences rather than treating every field as equivalent. The usual variety provided a relevant local reference. A promising candidate needed to be judged against what farmers could already grow, not simply against the performance of other unfamiliar samples. Early maturity and a large harvest were recorded separately so that one favorable result would not hide a tradeoff.

The first season produced no universal winner. One candidate matured earlier but yielded less under the trial conditions. Another performed well at a farm with different soil and water management, leaving uncertainty about which difference explained the result. Farmers contributed observations about handling and harvest that the original collection labels had not captured. Staff treated these observations as information to document and test, rather than either dismissing them as informal or accepting them as proof of broad suitability. A second season could examine whether the patterns persisted when weather changed.

The bank's preservation work continued alongside the trials. Stored samples needed to remain identifiable and capable of producing plants, and trial records had to remain linked to the correct material. Evaluation did not replace conservation: a sample with little immediate local use might become useful under different conditions or for future breeding. Conservation did not replace evaluation either. A long catalog of living material could preserve options without giving farmers enough information to choose among them. The two activities protected different parts of the same opportunity.

The farmer's initial question thus generated knowledge more useful than a simple recommendation based on origin. The bank could report which candidates matured early in the observed conditions, how their yields compared, and which uncertainties remained. It could not guarantee performance in every future season. The general lesson was that genetic diversity becomes practically accessible when stored material is connected to trustworthy descriptions and relevant experience. Local trials, careful records, and continued preservation allow that connection to develop without reducing a varied collection to a single supposedly climate-ready crop.

questions.stem: Why was the dry-region label insufficient to answer the farmer's question?
questions.stem_ja: 「乾燥地域」というラベルだけでは農家の問いに答えられなかったのはなぜか。

choices.text: It omitted yield because collection records focused on early maturity.
choices.text_ja: 採集記録が早く実ることに重点を置いていたため、収量が記されていなかったから。

choices.text: It described a sample that the bank had preserved mainly for breeding rather than cultivation.
choices.text_ja: シードバンクが栽培用ではなく、主に品種改良用に保存していた試料を示していたから。

choices.text: It identified a collection location without establishing performance under the farmer's specific conditions.
choices.text_ja: 採集場所は特定していたが、農家の具体的な条件のもとでの成績を明らかにしていなかったから。

choices.text: It showed that the variety survived dryness by taking longer to mature.
choices.text_ja: その品種が、実るまでの期間を長くすることで乾燥を生き延びることを示していたから。

questions.stem: Why distinguish early maturity from continued growth through a dry period?
questions.stem_ja: 早く実ることと、乾燥期の間も育ち続けることを区別するのはなぜか。

choices.text: They can address different timing problems despite sharing a broad description related to dryness.
choices.text_ja: どちらも乾燥に関わる大まかな説明に当てはまるが、異なる時期の問題に対応しうるから。

choices.text: The distinction determines which samples should be removed from conservation.
choices.text_ja: その区別によって、どの試料を保存の対象から外すべきかが決まるから。

choices.text: Both strategies require the same season length but different planting records.
choices.text_ja: どちらの戦略も同じ生育期間の長さを必要とするが、植えつけの記録が異なるから。

choices.text: The first indicates lower yield, while the second indicates adaptation to every dry region.
choices.text_ja: 前者は収量が少ないことを示し、後者はあらゆる乾燥地域への適応を示すから。

questions.stem: Why include each farm's usual variety in the trial?
questions.stem_ja: 各農場のいつもの品種を試験に含めたのはなぜか。

choices.text: To reduce the need to record differences in management between farms.
choices.text_ja: 農場間の管理方法の違いを記録する必要を減らすため。

choices.text: To provide a local reference for judging whether a candidate offers an advantage.
choices.text_ja: 候補品種に利点があるかどうかを判断するための、地元における比較基準とするため。

choices.text: To ensure that unfamiliar varieties are grown under identical weather across the region.
choices.text_ja: なじみのない品種を、地域全体で同一の天候のもとで栽培できるようにするため。

choices.text: To combine maturity and yield into a single measure of success.
choices.text_ja: 実る時期と収量を一つの成功の尺度にまとめるため。

questions.stem: A candidate performs best at one farm with different soil and management. What is justified?
questions.stem_ja: ある候補品種が、土壌と管理方法の異なる一つの農場で最もよい成績を上げた。正当といえるのはどれか。

choices.text: The result should be excluded because the farms were not identical.
choices.text_ja: 農場が同一ではなかったので、その結果は除外すべきである。

choices.text: The candidate should become the bank's preferred recommendation for the region.
choices.text_ja: その候補を、シードバンクがその地域に推奨する第一の品種とすべきである。

choices.text: The soil difference explains its advantage more convincingly than management does.
choices.text_ja: その品種の優位性は、管理方法よりも土壌の違いによってより説得力をもって説明できる。

choices.text: The result is promising evidence tied to those conditions, requiring further comparisons.
choices.text_ja: その結果は、その条件に結びついた有望な証拠であり、さらに比較が必要である。

questions.stem: How do conservation and evaluation complement each other?

passage.title: Why Better Forecasts May Not Change Behavior

paragraphs.text: Would a more accurate forecast make the same people take protective action? The question can be tested only if forecast performance and human response are measured separately. Imagine a warning about severe weather that correctly identifies the affected area, yet some residents remain where they are. It would be tempting to conclude that they failed to understand the information. That is one possibility, but it is not the only one. A person may understand a warning and still lack transport, doubt who is responsible for helping, or face consequences that the forecast itself does not describe.

Forecast accuracy concerns how predictions correspond to events under an appropriate method of assessment. Action concerns what someone does with information in a particular situation. Better predictions can improve the basis for decisions, but they do not automatically supply the means to carry them out. Even understanding involves several steps. A message must reach its intended recipient, be interpreted, and connect the predicted event to a relevant decision. A forecast stated in technical terms may be accurate yet leave a resident unsure about what it implies for the place where they live.

Trust is another category, distinct from both accuracy and comprehension. Someone may understand a message but question its source, especially if earlier communications seemed inconsistent or were poorly explained. A previous warning followed by little local damage does not by itself establish that the warning was unreasonable; protective decisions often concern uncertain outcomes. Nevertheless, the experience can affect how a later message is received. Communicators therefore need to explain uncertainty consistently rather than allowing confidence in the system to depend on every individual warning appearing correct in retrospect.

Practical capacity introduces a different barrier. Consider two hypothetical residents who accept the same warning. One has an available vehicle and somewhere to go. The other must arrange assistance for a dependent relative and has no transport. Sending the second resident a more precise prediction does not supply that missing assistance. Responsibility can also be unclear: a resident may expect a support service to call, while the service expects residents to request help. Both sides can possess the warning without coordinating the action. The missing link is an arrangement, not a weather measurement.

Different forms of communication can address some of these gaps. A technical probability may be useful to a planner choosing among operational options, while a public message may need to explain likely local effects, timing, and the relevant official instructions. This does not require hiding uncertainty or giving everyone the same wording. It requires matching the information to the decision without changing what the evidence supports. Testing whether recipients can explain the message in their own words can reveal comprehension problems that a count of delivered notifications would miss.

Information delivery and practical support should consequently be assessed together but not confused. Clearer wording may improve understanding while leaving transport barriers unchanged. A support arrangement may enable action without altering the forecast's accuracy. In a hypothetical evaluation, investigators could ask whether people received and understood a warning, whether help was available, and what they then did. Comparing these stages helps locate a failure more precisely than classifying everyone who remained as unwilling. It also avoids treating an increase in message reach as though it necessarily represented an increase in protection.

The initial question therefore has a conditional answer. Improved forecasts can support better decisions when communication, trust, and the capacity to act allow their information to be used. The categories interact: reliable help can make an instruction more credible, and a clear message can make support easier to request. Yet their differences remain useful because they point to different remedies. Forecast skill is an essential technical achievement, not a complete measure of an effective warning system. Evaluating that system requires following information far enough to see whether people could turn it into the intended protective action.

passage.title: The Forgotten Cost of a Trading Empire

paragraphs.text: Whose prosperity can be reconstructed from a merchant's ledger? A page recording cargo sales, payments, and profit offers unusually precise evidence, but its precision has boundaries. Imagine using such accounts to describe a port within a maritime trading empire. The figures might reveal growing commercial returns while saying little about the people who loaded ships or spent months at sea. This is not a claim about an invented surviving document. It is a way to examine how the purpose of a historical source shapes the story that can reasonably be built from it.

Merchants needed accounts to track transactions, debts, and the performance of ventures. Those needs encouraged the recording of quantities and payments that mattered to the business. A wage could appear as an expense without describing the work required to earn it. A profitable voyage might therefore be documented in detail from the investor's perspective while remaining poorly described from a sailor's. The account need not be deliberately false to produce this imbalance. A source designed for one practical task can become misleading when used to answer a much broader question without recognizing what it was never intended to record.

A trading empire's wealth was also distributed among groups with different powers and opportunities. Increased returns to merchants do not directly establish improved conditions for dock workers or crews. Even a recorded rise in wages would need interpretation alongside prices, employment duration, and the burdens attached to the work. The relevant distinction is between the amount of wealth generated and the way its benefits and costs were shared. These questions connect, but an answer to the first cannot simply be extended to the second.

Other records can broaden the inquiry. A labor agreement may state pay, responsibilities, or the length of service. It shows the terms offered or accepted, but does not necessarily prove that those terms were fulfilled. A court record can reveal a dispute about payment or treatment, though disputes reaching a court may differ from experiences that left no legal trace. A personal letter may describe fears or working conditions in a way an account does not, yet its writer represents a particular position and may have reasons for emphasizing some details. Each source opens a view while introducing its own limits.

Consider a hypothetical comparison involving one voyage. The merchant's account lists a payment for wages, a crew agreement promises payment at a stated point, and a later complaint alleges that part of the money was withheld. Together, the records create a more specific question than any one source alone: who actually received what, and when? The complaint does not automatically overturn the account. The account's total does not automatically settle the complaint either. Investigators would need to examine what the payment entry covered and whether the documents concern the same people and period.

Survival of evidence creates a further difficulty. Records kept by well-established institutions may be more available than private accounts from people with fewer resources. Finding more merchant documents than worker letters cannot be treated as proof that merchant experience was more representative. Nor can a few vivid accounts of hardship be used to calculate how frequently that hardship occurred across an empire. Historians can identify missing perspectives, compare available sources, and state the limits of a claim. They cannot recover an exact balance merely by giving each surviving document equal weight.

The ledger remains valuable after this wider examination. Its figures can establish aspects of trade that would otherwise be difficult to reconstruct. What changes is the claim made on their basis. Commercial growth becomes one part of an account that also asks about labor, payment, risk, and unequal access to benefits. The opening question can therefore be answered more precisely: a merchant's ledger describes prosperity through the transactions it was built to track. Reconstructing the wider cost of a trading system requires other evidence and an explicit recognition of whose experiences remain only partly visible.

passage.title: The Hidden Price of Too Many Choices

paragraphs.text: The fictional town of Norvale added more appointment options to its public-service website, yet a larger share of visitors left without completing an application. The expanded list included evenings and different locations, changes intended to help residents find a suitable arrangement. Some users welcomed the flexibility; others stopped at the selection screen. Officials initially described the result as evidence that too much choice discouraged people. Their data supported a narrower observation: completion had fallen after the redesign. To identify why, they needed to examine what else had changed and what the unfinished applications could reveal.

More options can provide a real benefit. A resident with an unusual work schedule may need a time that a shorter list excludes. Someone dependent on a particular bus route may value a less central office. Reducing the list could make comparison easier while removing the arrangement that fits such users. The relevant problem was therefore not simply the number of choices. It involved how residents could recognize useful options and compare their consequences. A wide range that is difficult to navigate can offer formal freedom without making that freedom equally usable.

The new screen placed many appointments in one long list. Each entry combined location, time, eligibility conditions, and service details in text of similar appearance. Users often needed to remember one entry while scrolling to compare it with another. This provided a plausible explanation for delay, especially for people unsure which differences mattered. It did not establish that everyone leaving the page was confused. Some might have been checking availability before applying later, and others might have discovered that the required documents were unavailable. A departure was a recorded action, not a direct measurement of its cause.

Norvale designed a fictional trial to separate two changes. One version grouped the same appointments by location and then by time. Another retained the original order but shortened the initial descriptions, allowing users to open further details. A third retained the existing screen for comparison. Visitors were assigned to versions in a way intended to create comparable groups, and the range of available appointments remained the same. This mattered because a simpler screen with fewer options would otherwise mix the effect of presentation with the effect of losing choices.

The grouped version produced a higher completion rate during the trial. Officials also examined whether users selected suitable services and whether later corrections increased. A quick selection that led to the wrong appointment would not represent the same improvement as a successful application. Feedback from users who completed the process added information about satisfaction, but it left out people who departed. The team therefore invited feedback from some of those users as well. Even then, respondents might differ from people who ignored the invitation, so their comments were treated as evidence rather than a complete account of every departure.

The result supported changing the presentation more clearly than reducing the available range. It did not demonstrate that offering additional options would always be harmless, or that grouping would work equally well for a different service. The trial occurred with a particular set of appointments and users. Officials also noticed that grouping by location helped residents who knew where they wanted to go, while users focused on the earliest available time needed a different way to view the list. The final design offered both views without requiring the full descriptive text to remain visible at once.

Norvale's experience distinguished several outcomes that the phrase 'better choice' had combined. A broader range could improve fit, clearer organization could reduce comparison effort, and successful completion could still differ from later satisfaction. The trial left uncertainty about longer-term use and less frequent users' needs. It did establish that the first decline in completion was insufficient grounds for removing options. Making choice usable required attention to how alternatives were presented and evaluated, rather than assuming that either a longer or a shorter list was inherently more respectful of residents' freedom.

passage.title: A Water Treaty Under Pressure

paragraphs.text: The fictional countries of Upper Vale and Lowland continued receiving their agreed shares of a river, but neither received enough water for its usual plans. A prolonged dry period had reduced the total flow. The treaty's fixed percentages still divided the available amount correctly, while the amounts themselves had become much smaller. Upstream farmers faced reduced irrigation, and downstream communities saw pressure on both crops and the river environment. The disagreement was not initially about a broken calculation. It concerned whether a rule designed for predictability could address conditions under which correct division no longer met essential needs.

When the treaty was negotiated, a common ratio had offered an advantage over repeated seasonal bargaining. Each government could estimate its allocation from the measured flow, and neither could easily claim a larger share merely by changing its stated demand. Farmers and water managers planned around that stability. The agreement also reflected a particular balance of uses and expectations at the time. Calling the ratio fair combined two claims: the rule treated the countries consistently, and the resulting allocations were acceptable. Reduced flow exposed how those claims could come apart.

At an upstream farming meeting, growers emphasized the investments they had made under the treaty. Crops already planted could not be changed as easily as next season's choices, and a sudden reduction beyond the agreed share could impose concentrated losses. Downstream, officials pointed to water needed to sustain river functions as well as withdrawals for farms and households. A percentage could shrink below an amount necessary for a particular purpose. Their concern was not answered simply by observing that the upstream country had also lost water. Equal proportional losses could have different consequences for different uses.

The upstream government worried that a broad emergency exception would make its share uncertain whenever the downstream country claimed hardship. The downstream government worried that strict adherence would protect the rule while allowing serious damage to continue. Both concerns affected trust. A flexible clause could address unusual conditions, but if either side defined those conditions alone, flexibility could become a means of changing the bargain without genuine agreement. Conversely, a clause so difficult to activate that it never operated during a severe shortage would add little practical protection.

Negotiators therefore considered specifying how an exception would begin, what evidence it required, and when normal rules would resume. Shared flow measurements could reduce disagreement about the size of the shortage. Agreed indicators could identify conditions requiring review, while monitoring could check whether temporary commitments were being followed. These arrangements would not create additional water or settle every dispute about priorities. They would make departures from the usual rule more transparent. A declared need would have to connect to common evidence and a defined process rather than function as a claim that automatically overruled the treaty.

Discussions also moved between immediate protection and future adjustment. An emergency allocation might address the current season without encouraging either country to plan for lower supplies later. Investments, crop choices, and water-use practices could influence future vulnerability, but their benefits and costs would not appear equally or immediately. The governments therefore distinguished temporary measures from changes to the longer-term agreement. They also acknowledged that water needed for river functions was not simply another country's consumption: maintaining those functions could matter across the border, even though the short-term costs of reducing withdrawals fell in particular places.

The negotiation did not end with a claim that one ratio or emergency formula was fair under every condition. The observable problem was that a declining total had made the old shares inadequate for important uses. Choosing which uses to protect, and how to distribute unavoidable losses, remained a judgment requiring agreement. The proposed procedures made that judgment more accountable by connecting exceptions to shared evidence, monitoring, and an endpoint. Flexibility could support cooperation when it operated through rules both sides could examine; without those conditions, it risked becoming the uncertainty the original treaty had been designed to reduce.

passage.title: When City Lights Mislead Young Sea Turtles

paragraphs.text: From the height of a newly hatched sea turtle, a beach is a landscape of ridges, shadows, and distant light. Picture a hatchling emerging before dawn on a developed coast. Beyond one stretch of sand lies the open sea; behind another stand buildings with illuminated windows. The animal must begin a journey without an adult showing it the route. A human observer might assume that the water is an obvious destination. For a creature moving close to the ground, however, finding that destination depends on the information available from its immediate surroundings.

On a naturally dark beach, the open horizon over the sea is generally brighter and lower than the inland view, where dunes or vegetation can form dark shapes. Hatchlings respond to this visual contrast when moving toward the water. They are not simply following the moon, which need not be visible for them to find the sea. Nor does this behavior require them to understand what the bright area represents. A response that guides movement effectively in a natural setting can work because the arrangement of light and landscape usually provides useful directional information.

Artificial light can alter that arrangement. A landward light may draw hatchlings away from the water or make their paths less direct. Extra travel can increase their exposure to danger before they reach the sea. Yet the brightness of an individual lamp is not the whole issue. Its position, whether it is visible from the sand, and how it compares with the surrounding horizon also matter. A lamp that seems modest to a person standing on a walkway may remain prominent from a hatchling's lower viewpoint. Measuring light where people stand can therefore miss part of the problem.

The journey also includes a change of environment. Once hatchlings enter the water, wave movement can provide directional information, helping them swim away from shore. This does not mean that waves can correct a landward route while the animals are still crossing dry sand. Different cues become useful at different stages. Even within the beach stage, the shape of the shoreline and the presence of dunes or vegetation influence what the animal can see. Describing the entire journey as attraction to light leaves out both the surrounding landscape and the information available after entry into the sea.

Consider a hypothetical beach where managers lower the brightness of lights along a public path. Fewer hatchlings subsequently travel inland. That observation is encouraging, but it does not prove that every remaining difficulty is caused by insufficient dimming. Some lights may still be visible through gaps, and physical obstacles may affect the route independently of lighting. Nor would improved movement across the sand establish that survival later in the ocean has improved by the same amount. To evaluate the change, managers need observations tied to the stage and outcome they are trying to influence, rather than a single claim about survival. They could record where routes turn inland and where animals encounter obstructions. If difficulties cluster near an exposed window, that pattern suggests a different response from difficulties beside a barrier. Such observations help distinguish explanations that would look similar in a total count alone.

Practical decisions must also consider people using the coast after dark. Path lighting serves a purpose, so a useful assessment asks where illumination is needed and where it spreads unnecessarily. Shielding a light or changing its position can reduce its visibility from the beach while retaining light on a walking surface. Such arrangements still need checking from the sand: a design that works beside one dune may be exposed along another section. The lesson from the hatchling's journey is therefore specific. Conservation should preserve reliable directional information in the setting where animals use it, and judge interventions by relevant observations. Reducing artificial light can be an important part of that work, but the animal navigates through a changing combination of light, landscape, and water.

passage.title: The Trial of a Ship's Missing Cargo

paragraphs.text: A list of missing crates lies on the court's table beside an invoice and a sea captain's journal. In this fictional dispute set in a nineteenth-century port, a merchant demands payment for goods that did not arrive. The documents agree that a shipment was expected, but they describe its size and its losses differently. The court's central question is not simply whether something is missing. It must determine which goods entered the carrier's care, what happened during the voyage, and which losses fall within the responsibility established by the parties' agreement.

The merchant's invoice lists the goods sold to an overseas buyer. He treats its total as the amount placed aboard the vessel. A warehouse clerk, however, explains that invoices were prepared before loading and sometimes included packages sent on a later ship. The invoice is genuine, but its original purpose was to record a sale rather than to certify loading. A separate receipt signed at the dock lists fewer crates. This discrepancy weakens the claim that the full invoice quantity was carried, without showing that either document was deliberately false.

The captain's journal describes a storm and records that cargo was thrown overboard to reduce danger. He argues that this accounts for the short delivery. Yet the entry groups the discarded goods broadly and does not identify every crate. The court compares it with a coastal weather record and testimony from sailors. These sources support the occurrence of severe weather. They cannot, by themselves, establish that each item on the merchant's missing list was among the goods sacrificed. Evidence for a dangerous event is not automatically evidence for the fate of a particular package.

The fictional contract provides an exception for cargo reasonably sacrificed to protect the vessel during an emergency. It also requires ordinary care in securing and protecting the goods. These terms are invented for this case, not presented as a universal rule of nineteenth-century maritime law. Under them, showing that a storm occurred would not settle responsibility. The court would still need to ask whether a claimed sacrifice met the exception and whether a different loss resulted from a failure of care before or during the storm.

One sailor recalls damaged lashings near a stack of crates before the worst weather arrived. Another remembers that the same area was checked and repaired. Their accounts initially appear incompatible, but the timing matters: an inspection followed by repairs could make both memories accurate. The court asks when each observation occurred and which part of the hold each sailor could see. Neither witness had a complete view of the cargo throughout the voyage. Treating confidence of delivery as a substitute for opportunity to observe would hide those limits.

The comparison produces a narrower account than either side first offered. The loading receipt supports a smaller starting quantity than the invoice, and several crates can be connected to the recorded emergency sacrifice through identifying marks described by witnesses. Other losses remain uncertain. For those, the court needs evidence connecting the missing goods to either an allowed sacrifice or a breach of the care requirement. It cannot distribute every unexplained crate among convenient categories merely to make the totals balance. The remaining uncertainty is itself part of the historical record.

A historian reading this imagined trial would therefore distinguish the final legal decision from a complete reconstruction of the voyage. A decision must apply the relevant agreement and standards of proof to the evidence available; it need not explain everything that happened at sea. The documents become most informative when their purposes, timing, and limits are examined together. Their disagreements reveal different stages of a shipment's history. Rather than identify a villain from one inconsistency, the inquiry establishes which claims can be supported, which are weakened, and which questions remain open.
