passage.title: The Jury That Changed Its View Twice

paragraphs.text: Most members initially favor removing a low wall from the fictional town of Norbridge's public square. They believe an open layout will make the space more welcoming. The group is a residents' jury assembled to study a proposed renovation and advise the council; it is not a criminal court. Before meeting specialists, members record their preferred option and their reasons. The opening vote gives organizers a baseline, but it does not establish which plan is best or how deeply members have considered its consequences.

An access specialist then challenges the majority's assumption. The wall narrows one route, she agrees, but it also separates a walking area from a change in ground level. Removing it without redesigning the surface could create a new difficulty. Her diagrams compare a simple removal with a more extensive alteration. Several members had imagined that removing the wall would solve both crowding and access problems at little additional cost. The new information separates those expectations: an open square and an accessible square may require overlapping but different work.

In a second informal vote, support shifts toward keeping the wall. Some members cite the diagrams; others are concerned about the cost of the broader redesign. Counting changed votes alone would hide these different reasons. It might also exaggerate the specialist's final influence because her presentation is the latest information the group has heard. The facilitator therefore asks members to write what changed their minds and which questions remain. This creates a record that can later distinguish a revised understanding from a temporary response to a persuasive speaker.

A resident who uses the square daily offers another challenge. The existing wall channels people toward a crowded corner where delivery vehicles sometimes obstruct the passage. Keeping it unchanged would preserve that difficulty. A shopkeeper confirms the delivery pattern but worries that moving vehicle access would harm nearby businesses. Their testimony does not invalidate the specialist's account of the ground level. It adds conditions missing from the diagrams and shows that the choice is not simply between a risky removal and a satisfactory existing arrangement.

The jury requests a revised option that retains protection at the change in level while creating a wider walking route and adjusting delivery times. It also asks for costs and practical objections to be presented together. This matters because presenting benefits first and costs much later can encourage comparisons based on unequal information. The facilitator gives each option the same discussion period and invites members who have spoken little to contribute. Equal time does not guarantee equal evidence, but it reduces one avoidable source of imbalance in the process.

The final vote divides the group again. A majority now favors the revised arrangement, while a minority doubts whether delivery-time changes can be enforced. The recommendation includes both the preferred plan and that objection, with a request for a trial of the delivery arrangements before permanent construction. Some members have changed position twice; others have kept their original view for different reasons. The final count by itself cannot reveal these paths. Written explanations show whether members have addressed new evidence or simply repeated their initial preferences.

Evaluating the jury therefore requires more than measuring agreement. The council can ask whether relevant experiences were heard, assumptions were examined, and alternatives received comparable scrutiny. It can also check whether the final proposal responds to the strongest objection rather than merely recording it politely. Norbridge's changing votes are not automatic proof of confusion, just as its final majority is not proof of wisdom. Their value depends on the reasons and procedures behind them. A recommendation can become more useful through disagreement when that disagreement identifies a condition the town must test before acting.

questions.stem: Which initial assumption did the specialist's presentation undermine?
questions.stem_ja: 専門家の発表によって崩れたのは、どの当初の前提か。

choices.text: A more extensive redesign would change the square's layout.
choices.text_ja: より大がかりな改修を行えば、広場の配置が変わる。

choices.text: Simple wall removal would cheaply resolve both crowding and access concerns.
choices.text_ja: 塀を単純に撤去するだけで、混雑とバリアフリーの両方の懸念が安価に解決する。

choices.text: Opening the square would require considering people's movement through it.
choices.text_ja: 広場を開放的にするには、そこを通る人の動きを考慮する必要がある。

choices.text: The current wall affected the route used by pedestrians.
choices.text_ja: 現在の塀は、歩行者が使う通路に影響を与えている。

questions.stem: Why retain written reasons alongside vote counts?
questions.stem_ja: 票数とあわせて、書かれた理由を残しておくのはなぜか。

choices.text: They distinguish evidence-based cost concerns from experience-based concerns that should receive less weight.
choices.text_ja: 証拠に基づく費用面の懸念と、より軽く扱うべき経験に基づく懸念とを区別できるから。

choices.text: They turn unchanged votes into evidence that no learning occurred.
choices.text_ja: 票が変わらなかったことを、何も学ばれなかったことの証拠にできるから。

choices.text: They reveal different reasoning paths hidden by the same numerical result.
choices.text_ja: 同じ数値の結果の陰に隠れた、異なる考えの道筋が明らかになるから。

choices.text: They allow organizers to infer that the latest speaker caused every changed vote.
choices.text_ja: 主催者が、票の変化はすべて最後の発言者によるものだと推論できるから。

questions.stem: How does the resident's testimony relate to the specialist's analysis?
questions.stem_ja: 住民の証言は、専門家の分析とどのような関係にあるか。

choices.text: It replaces the need to compare the wider redesign with simple removal.
choices.text_ja: 大がかりな改修と単純な撤去とを比較する必要をなくしている。

choices.text: It establishes that removing the wall would resolve business concerns.
choices.text_ja: 塀を撤去すれば店の懸念が解消されることを立証している。

choices.text: It explains the ground-level warning as a consequence of delivery practices missing from the diagrams.
choices.text_ja: 段差についての警告を、図には欠けていた配送の実態から生じたものとして説明している。

choices.text: It adds a practical problem without disproving the warning about ground level.
choices.text_ja: 段差についての警告を否定することなく、実際上の問題を付け加えている。

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of presenting costs and benefits together for every option?
questions.stem_ja: すべての案について費用と利点をまとめて示すことの主な目的は何か。

choices.text: To preserve the order in which the original proposals gained support.
choices.text_ja: もとの案が支持を集めた順序を保つため。

choices.text: To reduce comparisons distorted by uneven timing and completeness of information.
choices.text_ja: 情報が示される時期や完全さの偏りによって比較がゆがむのを減らすため。

choices.text: To stabilize the second vote before members hear further objections to keeping the wall.
choices.text_ja: 塀を残すことへのさらなる反対意見を聞く前に、2回目の投票結果を固めるため。

choices.text: To ensure that equal speaking time produces equally strong evidence.
choices.text_ja: 発言時間を平等にすることで、同じくらい強い証拠が得られるようにするため。

questions.stem: Which action best responds to the final minority objection?
questions.stem_ja: 最終投票での少数派の反対意見に最もよく応えている対応はどれか。

choices.text: Test whether the delivery schedule can be enforced before permanent work.
choices.text_ja: 恒久的な工事の前に、配送時間の取り決めを守らせることができるかを試す。

choices.text: Ask members to agree on the initial wall-removal proposal for consistency.
choices.text_ja: 一貫性を保つため、メンバーに最初の塀撤去案に同意するよう求める。

choices.text: Repeat the original vote after removing the cost information.
choices.text_ja: 費用の情報を取り除いたうえで、最初の投票をやり直す。

choices.text: Record the objection and proceed because the revised plan won a majority.
choices.text_ja: 修正案が多数派の支持を得たので、反対意見を記録したうえで計画を進める。

passage.title: The Quietest Seat in a Concert Hall

paragraphs.text: A listener near the stage hears the sharp beginning of each note, while someone farther away describes the same passage as a broad, blended sound. These impressions need not mean that either listener has judged the performance poorly. The sound reaching a seat depends on several paths, and the qualities a person values may differ. Even calling a seat quiet leaves questions open. It might receive less musical energy, offer little background noise, or make a particular instrument less prominent. Those are different descriptions with different explanations.

The most direct path runs from an instrument to the listener without a reflection from a room surface. Distance and obstacles affect that contribution. Being close can make certain details stand out, but closeness to the stage is not closeness to every player. A listener beside one section may hear a different balance from someone facing the orchestra more centrally. Instruments also send sound outward differently depending on direction and frequency. A seat's relationship to the sources therefore matters alongside its simple distance from the stage edge.

Other sound reaches the listener after reflecting from walls, the ceiling, or other surfaces. Reflections arriving soon after the direct sound can support it and influence the impression of space. Later sound contributes to the lingering effect called reverberation. The timing, strength, and direction of these arrivals matter, not merely their existence. Reflections are not automatically unwanted noise. They can enrich musical experience, although a combination that blends sustained tones attractively may make rapid details harder to distinguish. The relevant balance depends partly on the music.

The shape and materials around a particular seat affect which paths reach it. A position beneath a deep balcony may receive a different mixture from an exposed position farther forward. This does not supply a universal rule that one location is worse: the result depends on the hall's actual design. Audience members and seats also absorb and scatter sound, so an empty rehearsal space can differ from the same room during a full performance. A judgment based on a quick visit to an empty hall may therefore describe conditions unlike those of the intended concert.

Stage arrangement adds another layer. Moving an instrument changes its distance and orientation relative to listeners and reflecting surfaces. An acoustic measurement made from one source position cannot fully represent a whole orchestra distributed across the stage. Researchers can use several source locations to study these relationships and record how the room responds over time. Such measurements help distinguish sound level, clarity, and spatial effects. Combining them into a single seat ranking, however, requires decisions about how much importance to give each quality.

Listeners make those decisions differently. Someone following a complex line may favor separation and detail; another may value the surrounding, blended impression of a large ensemble. Preferences can also change with the program rather than remain fixed characteristics of the person. Controlled listening comparisons can investigate these responses, provided differences in performance or recording do not get mistaken for differences in the room. Measuring a seat and asking whether people like it answer related questions, but neither question can simply substitute for the other.

The search for the quietest seat is thus useful when the desired experience is specified. A person seeking less intensity may accept a different balance from one seeking the clearest quiet passage. Information about measured conditions can guide that choice without claiming to identify a seat that is best for every listener and piece. The hall is part of the performance's delivery, and each position samples that delivery differently. Understanding direct sound, reflected sound, and musical balance turns a vague ranking of seats into a more informative account of what a listener may hear and why.

questions.stem: Why is distance from the stage edge an incomplete guide to musical balance?
questions.stem_ja: 舞台の端からの距離が、音楽のバランスを知る手がかりとして不完全なのはなぜか。

choices.text: The sound level at a seat indicates the contribution made by each instrument separately.
choices.text_ja: 席での音量は、それぞれの楽器が個別にどれだけ寄与しているかを示すから。

choices.text: The seat has different distances and angles to different instruments.
choices.text_ja: その席から各楽器までの距離や角度は、楽器ごとに異なるから。

choices.text: Reflections compensate for instrument position, making the nearest section less relevant to balance.
choices.text_ja: 反射音が楽器の位置を補うので、最も近い楽器群はバランスにあまり関係しなくなるから。

choices.text: Moving closer increases detail from each orchestral section by roughly the same amount.
choices.text_ja: 近づくと、オーケストラの各楽器群から聞こえる細部がほぼ同じだけ増えるから。

questions.stem: Why might two listeners disagree about a reverberant sound without either misunderstanding it?
questions.stem_ja: 残響の多い音について、どちらも誤解していないのに二人の聴き手の意見が分かれることがあるのはなぜか。

choices.text: One may value blending while another values separation of rapid details.
choices.text_ja: 一方は音の溶け合いを重視し、もう一方は速い細部の分離を重視しているかもしれないから。

choices.text: A listener who prefers blending is probably hearing more direct sound from the nearest section.
choices.text_ja: 溶け合いを好む聴き手は、おそらく最も近い楽器群からの直接音をより多く聞いているから。

choices.text: Clear rapid details indicate that the room adds less useful musical support than a reverberant seat.
choices.text_ja: 速い細部が明瞭に聞こえることは、残響の多い席よりも部屋による音楽への有益な支えが少ないことを示すから。

choices.text: Blending provides a more direct measure of the hall's quality than separation does.
choices.text_ja: 溶け合いのほうが、分離よりもホールの質を直接的に測る尺度になるから。

questions.stem: What limits a seat assessment made during a brief visit to an empty hall?
questions.stem_ja: 空のホールを短時間訪れて行った席の評価には、どのような限界があるか。

choices.text: A short visit captures the hall's clarity more reliably than its intensity during performance.
choices.text_ja: 短時間の訪問では、演奏中の音の強さよりもホールの明瞭さのほうが確実にとらえられる。

choices.text: Empty-room measurements emphasize the direct sources rather than the reflected paths that dominate a concert.
choices.text_ja: 空の部屋での測定では、演奏会で支配的な反射音の経路よりも、直接の音源のほうが強調される。

choices.text: The balcony's position provides a stable substitute for measurements under occupied conditions.
choices.text_ja: バルコニーの位置は、観客が入った状態での測定の代わりとして安定して使える。

choices.text: Audience absorption and scattering may alter the concert conditions.
choices.text_ja: 観客による吸音や散乱によって、演奏会の条件が変わる可能性がある。

questions.stem: Why use multiple source positions when studying orchestral sound?
questions.stem_ja: オーケストラの音を研究する際に、複数の音源の位置を使うのはなぜか。

choices.text: The source locations identify which seats need the same weighting of clarity and intensity.
choices.text_ja: 音源の位置から、明瞭さと音の強さに同じ重みづけが必要な席が分かるから。

choices.text: Several positions allow researchers to average away source differences and measure listener preference.
choices.text_ja: 複数の位置を使えば、研究者は音源の違いを平均して打ち消し、聴き手の好みを測ることができるから。

choices.text: Changing source positions separates the room from every effect of the instruments.
choices.text_ja: 音源の位置を変えれば、楽器によるあらゆる影響から部屋を切り離せるから。

choices.text: One source cannot represent the different paths from a distributed orchestra.
choices.text_ja: 一つの音源では、舞台に広がるオーケストラからのさまざまな経路を表すことができないから。

questions.stem: Which seat description would be most useful to a listener choosing for a particular program?
questions.stem_ja: 特定の演目に合わせて席を選ぶ聴き手にとって、最も役に立つ席の説明はどれか。

choices.text: A single quality score calculated without explaining its priorities.
choices.text_ja: 何を優先したかを説明せずに算出された、一つの品質スコア。

choices.text: The preference of one listener presented as the hall's measured response.
choices.text_ja: ホールの測定された反応として示された、一人の聴き手の好み。

choices.text: Measured clarity and intensity with an explanation of the likely balance.
choices.text_ja: 測定された明瞭さと音の強さに、想定されるバランスの説明を添えたもの。

choices.text: A ranking based on the closest point of the stage edge.
choices.text_ja: 舞台の端に最も近い地点を基準にしたランキング。

passage.title: The Average Speed That Hid a Delay

paragraphs.text: The official graph rises: average bus speed on a route in the fictional city of Eastford has improved. The transport office presents the change as evidence that recent adjustments are working. Yet some passengers say their journeys take longer. The apparent contradiction becomes less mysterious when the office explains its calculation. It divides the distance traveled by buses by their recorded operating time along the route, including scheduled stops. Walking to the stop, waiting before boarding, and time spent transferring are outside that measure.

The improvement is therefore a claim about a defined part of travel, not necessarily a false claim. Fewer stops and changes to traffic signals can reduce time spent on the bus. A passenger traveling between retained stops may benefit directly. But removing a stop can also require another passenger to walk farther. The same operating change can improve the published number while creating a cost beyond its boundary. Evaluating the policy requires following both effects rather than treating either the favorable graph or the unfavorable account as sufficient by itself.

Consider two hypothetical passengers in Eastford. One lives beside a retained stop and rides directly to work. The other used a stop that has been removed and changes buses farther along the route. Their time inside the first bus can fall by the same amount, while their total journeys change differently. For the second passenger, extra walking may consume the gain before waiting is counted. An average over all riders can describe the overall pattern, but it may hide which neighborhoods or kinds of journey gained and which lost.

Waiting introduces a further distinction between a timetable and experience. If services are less frequent, passengers who arrive without matching a departure may wait longer even though each bus moves faster. Irregular service can also create long gaps followed by several buses close together. A simple average across departures may understate the experience of riders who accumulate during a long gap. Recording waiting from the passenger's perspective, including how many people face each delay, addresses a different question from measuring vehicle performance.

Transfers can amplify small changes in timing. A faster first bus helps when it reaches a connection before departure; a changed schedule can instead leave a passenger just after the connecting bus has gone. The consequence depends on coordination and the interval until the next service. Two routes may each show improved operating speed while the trip between them becomes less convenient. The transport office therefore examines complete itineraries and records whether connections are made, rather than assuming that separate improvements add together automatically.

To compare the old and new arrangements, Eastford proposes door-to-door journey records for different trip types and times of day. It includes walking, waiting, riding, and transferring, and reports typical times alongside the frequency of unusually long journeys. The comparison should use similar travel periods or account for differences such as school holidays and road works. Otherwise, a quiet week could be mistaken for a lasting improvement. Sampling should also include passengers from removed stops, since surveying people already aboard at retained stops could miss those who have stopped using the route.

The city keeps its operating-speed measure because it still answers a useful management question. Alongside it, the new report presents passenger journey time, reliability, and differences across groups. A policy may then be judged as improving bus movement while requiring further work on access or connections. That is a more informative conclusion than declaring either the graph or the complaints wrong. Indicators become useful when their boundaries are visible. A faster bus can contribute to a better journey, but the contribution must be tested within the journey that people actually need to make.

questions.stem: How can the official speed improvement and longer passenger journeys both be accurate?
questions.stem_ja: 公式の速度向上と乗客の移動時間の増加が、どちらも正しいと言えるのはなぜか。

choices.text: The route's shorter operating time shows that complaints concern reliability rather than duration.
choices.text_ja: 路線の運行時間が短くなったことから、苦情が所要時間ではなく信頼性に関するものだと分かるから。

choices.text: The office measures walking time but omits time at scheduled stops.
choices.text_ja: 交通局は徒歩の時間は測っているが、決められた停留所での時間は除いているから。

choices.text: The graph averages vehicle performance while the complaints mainly reflect unusually slow buses.
choices.text_ja: グラフは車両の性能を平均したものだが、苦情は主に異常に遅いバスを反映しているから。

choices.text: The speed calculation excludes several parts of the passenger's complete journey.
choices.text_ja: 速度の計算では、乗客の移動全体のうちいくつかの部分が除かれているから。

questions.stem: Which passenger is most likely to benefit directly from fewer stops, before other changes are considered?
questions.stem_ja: ほかの変更を考慮する前の段階で、停留所の削減から直接恩恵を受ける可能性が最も高いのはどの乗客か。

choices.text: A direct rider living beside a retained stop.
choices.text_ja: 残された停留所のそばに住み、乗り換えなしで乗る人。

choices.text: Someone whose connection departs just before the first bus arrives.
choices.text_ja: 最初のバスが着く直前に、乗り継ぎのバスが出発してしまう人。

choices.text: A passenger who can now board a faster first bus but must make an uncoordinated connection.
choices.text_ja: より速くなった最初のバスに乗れるようになったが、連携していない乗り継ぎをしなければならない乗客。

choices.text: A rider whose removed local stop requires a longer walk and a transfer.
choices.text_ja: 最寄りの停留所が廃止されたため、より長く歩いて乗り換えなければならない乗客。

questions.stem: Why might an average across departures understate passengers' waiting experience?
questions.stem_ja: 発車ごとの平均が、乗客の待ち時間の体験を実際より軽く見積もってしまう可能性があるのはなぜか。

choices.text: The timetable gives planned departures rather than the average speed published by the office.
choices.text_ja: 時刻表が示すのは予定された発車時刻であって、交通局が公表している平均速度ではないから。

choices.text: More passengers may accumulate during long gaps and bear those delays.
choices.text_ja: 長い間隔の間には、より多くの乗客がたまり、その遅れを被ることになるかもしれないから。

choices.text: Passengers arriving during a gap can distribute themselves evenly among the following departures.
choices.text_ja: 間隔の間に来た乗客は、その後の各便に均等に分かれて乗ることができるから。

choices.text: The faster buses receive greater weight in departure averages because they carry fewer riders.
choices.text_ja: 速いバスは乗客が少ないので、発車ごとの平均で大きな重みを与えられるから。

questions.stem: Both bus routes become faster, but a transfer trip becomes slower. Which additional finding best explains this?
questions.stem_ja: 二つのバス路線はどちらも速くなったが、乗り換えを伴う移動は遅くなった。これを最もよく説明する追加の事実はどれか。

choices.text: The published figures combine direct riders with those making connections.
choices.text_ja: 公表された数値は、乗り換えなしの乗客と乗り継ぎをする乗客をまとめたものである。

choices.text: The second route's faster operating time comes from signal changes rather than removed stops.
choices.text_ja: 二つ目の路線の運行時間が短くなったのは、停留所の削減ではなく信号の調整によるものである。

choices.text: The first bus now reaches the connection just after its departure.
choices.text_ja: 最初のバスが、今では乗り継ぎのバスの出発直後に到着するようになった。

choices.text: The first route retains the passenger's local stop while removing intermediate stops.
choices.text_ja: 最初の路線では、途中の停留所は削減されたが、乗客の最寄りの停留所は残された。

questions.stem: Which comparison would best assess who benefits from the new arrangement?
questions.stem_ja: 新しい体制で誰が恩恵を受けるかを評価するのに、最も適した比較はどれか。

choices.text: Track complete journeys across trip types and include users affected by removed stops.
choices.text_ja: さまざまな種類の移動について全行程を追跡し、停留所の廃止の影響を受けた利用者も含める。

choices.text: Survey current riders at retained stops during one unusually quiet week.
choices.text_ja: 異常に空いていた一週間に、残された停留所で現在の乗客を調査する。

choices.text: Rank routes by operating speed and assign each rider the route average.
choices.text_ja: 路線を運行速度で順位づけし、各乗客にその路線の平均値を割り当てる。

choices.text: Compare the fastest new trip with the typical previous journey.
choices.text_ja: 新体制での最も速い移動を、以前の典型的な移動と比べる。

passage.title: The Fossil Found Far from Its Habitat

paragraphs.text: A shell fossil on a mountain path seems to put a sea creature in the wrong place. Imagine a walker finding one high above the nearest coast, where no present-day marine animal could live. The temptation is to explain the surprise immediately: perhaps the animal once lived on the mountain, or perhaps the sea once covered it. Both suggestions begin with the modern landscape. A geological investigation instead asks how the fossil, the rock containing it, and the landscape each reached their present condition.

The identification of the organism matters first. Features shared with organisms associated with shallow marine environments can support an interpretation of its living conditions. That is a different claim from saying that it lived at the exact point where the walker stands. Even before becoming a fossil, remains can be moved from the place where an animal lived to the place where they are buried. Thus, information about habitat and information about the location of burial should be related carefully rather than collapsed into one statement.

One explanation is that the rock formed from sediment deposited in a marine setting and was later raised as the Earth's crust changed. The present elevation would then belong to a later chapter than the organism's life. To support this account, investigators would look beyond the single shell. Other marine fossils within the same continuous rock layers, together with sediment features consistent with that setting, would strengthen the interpretation. The aim is to reconstruct the environment in which the material accumulated, not to imagine seawater occupying the mountain exactly as it looks today.

Evidence of folding, tilting, or other deformation can contribute to the later part of the story. If fossil-bearing layers can be traced through a wider area and their relationships fit movement of the crust, uplift becomes more than a convenient explanation for one surprising object. Still, a tilted layer alone does not give the complete sequence, rate, or date of its movement. Several processes can affect a landscape, and erosion removes parts of the record. A convincing reconstruction identifies which observations support each stage and where the timing remains uncertain.

There is also a competing explanation for the discovery itself. The walker may have found a loose piece of fossil-bearing stone transported from somewhere else. Natural movement or human activity could separate it from its original layer. In that case, the fossil might genuinely record a marine environment while saying little about the rock immediately beneath the path. Checking whether it is embedded in local bedrock, lies among loose fragments, or resembles material used in nearby construction would help distinguish these possibilities. Recording its position before removal is therefore part of the evidence, not merely a collector's detail.

The explanations need not be mutually exclusive at every scale. A marine rock may first have been raised with a mountain range and later broken off and moved onto the path. Evidence for transport would not erase its earlier marine history. It would change the confidence with which that history could be assigned to the exact discovery point. Conversely, finding many fossils fixed within continuous local layers would make a story based solely on a recently imported stone much less satisfactory. The strongest account is the one that explains the full pattern with the fewest unsupported steps.

The shell's unusual location consequently opens a sequence of questions instead of closing the case. Its form can inform an account of the organism; its surrounding sediment can inform an account of burial; the rock's relationships can inform an account of later movement. A carefully documented mountain fossil may contribute to a history of sea-floor deposition and uplift. A loose fragment may offer a less local history. Neither needs an invented date to be informative, provided that the difference between where something lived, where it was preserved, and where it was found remains clear.

questions.stem: Why is a marine identification insufficient to conclude that the animal lived at the discovery point?
questions.stem_ja: 海の生物だと特定できても、その動物が発見地点で暮らしていたと結論づけるには不十分なのはなぜか。

choices.text: Remains or fossil-bearing material may have moved between life, burial, and discovery.
choices.text_ja: 生きていた時、埋まった時、発見された時のあいだに、遺骸や化石を含む物質が移動した可能性があるから。

choices.text: Similar marine forms could place the surrounding sediment at the modern mountain's elevation.
choices.text_ja: 似た海の生物の形から、周囲の堆積物が現在の山の高さにあったとわかる可能性があるから。

choices.text: The fossil dates uplift more directly than the layer containing it dates marine deposition.
choices.text_ja: 化石は、それを含む地層が海での堆積の年代を示すよりも直接的に、隆起の年代を示すから。

choices.text: The identification describes burial conditions more precisely than the organism's living habitat.
choices.text_ja: 特定によってわかるのは、その生物が暮らしていた環境よりも、埋没の条件のほうが正確だから。

questions.stem: Which combination most strongly supports local marine deposition followed by later crustal movement?
questions.stem_ja: その土地での海での堆積と、その後の地殻の動きを最も強く裏づける組み合わせはどれか。

choices.text: A shell loose on the path and a distant account of marine fossils.
choices.text_ja: 山道に転がっている貝と、遠く離れた場所での海の化石についての報告。

choices.text: A tilted layer and a shell resembling stone used in nearby construction.
choices.text_ja: 傾いた地層と、近くの建設工事に使われた石に似た貝。

choices.text: Marine fossils within traceable local layers whose deformation fits regional crustal movement.
choices.text_ja: たどることのできる地元の地層に含まれる海の化石と、地域的な地殻の動きに合ったその地層の変形。

choices.text: Several loose shells and an unchanged modern coastline far below.
choices.text_ja: ばらばらの貝のいくつかと、はるか下にある変化していない現在の海岸線。

questions.stem: What different questions do layer deformation and the fossil's original find position help address?
questions.stem_ja: 地層の変形と、化石が最初に見つかった位置は、それぞれどのような異なる問いに答える助けになるか。

choices.text: Deformation supports a marine habitat; find position identifies the timing of uplift.
choices.text_ja: 変形は海でのすみかを裏づけ、発見位置は隆起の時期を特定する。

choices.text: Deformation connects the fragment to the path; find position reconstructs regional crustal motion.
choices.text_ja: 変形は破片を山道と結びつけ、発見位置は地域的な地殻の動きを再構成する。

choices.text: Deformation confirms local burial; find position distinguishes folding from later uplift.
choices.text_ja: 変形はその土地での埋没を確かめ、発見位置は褶曲とその後の隆起とを見分ける。

choices.text: Deformation informs later rock history; find position helps test the fossil's local association.
choices.text_ja: 変形は岩石のその後の歴史を知る手がかりとなり、発見位置は化石がその土地のものかどうかを検証する助けになる。

questions.stem: Suppose a loose fossil-bearing fragment was brought from another mountain. What conclusion remains possible?
questions.stem_ja: 化石を含むばらばらの破片が、別の山から運ばれてきたものだったとする。それでも成り立ちうる結論はどれか。

choices.text: The discovery point can be assigned the source mountain's complete history.
choices.text_ja: 発見地点に、運ばれてくる前の山の歴史のすべてを当てはめることができる。

choices.text: The fragment records marine history, but not necessarily that of the path's bedrock.
choices.text_ja: その破片は海の歴史を記録しているが、それが山道の基盤岩の歴史であるとは限らない。

choices.text: Its marine identification must be rejected because its local association failed.
choices.text_ja: その土地との結びつきが成り立たなかったので、海の生物だという特定は否定しなければならない。

choices.text: Its transport explanation replaces any earlier uplift explanation.
choices.text_ja: 運搬による説明が、それ以前の隆起による説明に完全に取って代わる。

questions.stem: Why does the author allow uplift and transport to be combined in one account?
questions.stem_ja: 筆者が、隆起と運搬を一つの説明の中で組み合わせることを認めているのはなぜか。

choices.text: Evidence of either process strengthens the fossil's connection to the exact discovery point.
choices.text_ja: どちらの過程の証拠も、化石とまさにその発見地点との結びつきを強めるから。

choices.text: Combining them makes the order of burial and later movement less important to the account.
choices.text_ja: 両者を組み合わせれば、埋没とその後の移動の順序が説明の中であまり重要でなくなるから。

choices.text: They can describe successive events rather than competing causes of the same stage.
choices.text_ja: 両者は、同じ段階をめぐって対立する原因ではなく、相次いで起きた出来事を表しうるから。

choices.text: Transport supplies the missing regional evidence whenever a local layer has been tilted.
choices.text_ja: その土地の地層が傾いている場合には、運搬が欠けている地域的な証拠を補うから。

passage.title: When Rival Inventors Shared a Patent

paragraphs.text: A replacement control unit fits one company's machine but cannot communicate with another's. In the fictional industry described here, customers must choose a family of products before they know which future components they may need. Two leading firms, Ardent and Vale, each own patents connected with the interface between devices. They compete to improve their products, yet disputes over those rights repeatedly interrupt development. Engineers spend time avoiding contested features, while customers wait for parts that could otherwise have worked together.

Initially, the firms treat incompatible designs as protection. Each hopes that customers who buy its main machine will return for compatible additions. This encourages investment in a distinctive product range, but it also limits the usefulness of improvements developed elsewhere. A buyer may prefer Ardent's machine and Vale's new controller without being able to combine them. Meanwhile, uncertainty over which design uses the other's patented method makes even an independently planned addition harder to bring to market.

The firms eventually negotiate a cross-licensing agreement for the relevant interface patents. Each receives permission to use specified technology belonging to the other, under agreed conditions. They also adopt a common connection standard for the products covered. The arrangement removes a defined obstacle between them; it does not turn every invention into freely available public property. Rights outside the agreement remain separate, and firms that did not sign it do not automatically receive the same permission. Those boundaries are central to what happens next.

During the following development cycle, Ardent and Vale introduce more compatible additions. Their engineers can work from a stable interface instead of redesigning around an unresolved dispute. Customers gain combinations that were previously unavailable. The firms still compete over reliability, service, and features outside the shared connection. Within this fictional case, cooperation at one layer supports competition at another. Yet the increase in products alone cannot tell an observer whether customers face stronger competitive pressure overall or simply a more convenient range controlled by the same two suppliers.

A smaller company, Mera, then proposes a specialized controller that would use the common interface. The standard makes it technically easier to design for both leading machines, which appears to lower an entry barrier. However, Mera also needs access to the covered technology. The fee offered to an outside licensee is large relative to its expected early sales, and approval depends on a process managed by the two established firms. A technical barrier has fallen while a contractual and financial barrier remains.

Ardent and Vale argue that contributions to development and testing deserve compensation. Mera replies that access terms can protect those contributions without placing a small entrant at a lasting disadvantage. An independent observer would need to examine the terms, their practical cost, and whether access decisions are applied consistently. Counting signed agreements would be less revealing than following what an entrant must do before selling a product. Similarly, counting compatible products would miss a potential loss if promising designs never reach the stage of a license application.

The case therefore has two comparisons across time. Customers can compare the earlier fragmented product families with the later compatible range. Potential entrants can compare the former technical difficulties with the new access requirements. Both comparisons may show improvements, but they need not improve by the same amount or for the same participants. A policy that judged cooperation solely by the output of the two signatories would overlook the conditions facing companies outside their arrangement.

Sharing the patents helped resolve a real development problem in this imagined industry. Whether the agreement also widened meaningful competition depends on how others can enter and what remains open to independent design. The proper question is neither whether rivals cooperated nor whether new products appeared. It is how the cooperation changed the opportunities to create, combine, and sell products for customers and firms inside and outside the agreement.

questions.stem: How did the agreement help development in the two leading firms?
questions.stem_ja: 契約は、大手二社の開発にどのように役立ったか。

choices.text: It transferred customers' future purchases to whichever company designed the main machine.
choices.text_ja: 顧客の将来の購入を、主力機械を設計した会社のほうへ移した。

choices.text: It made unrelated patents available to every company using the connection standard.
choices.text_ja: 接続規格を使うすべての企業が、関係のない特許も使えるようにした。

choices.text: It replaced competition over service with competition over interface ownership.
choices.text_ja: サービスをめぐる競争を、インターフェースの所有権をめぐる競争に置き換えた。

choices.text: It gave engineers defined permission and a stable interface for compatible additions.
choices.text_ja: 互換性のある追加製品のために、技術者に範囲の定まった許可と安定したインターフェースを与えた。

questions.stem: What explains Mera's mixed position after the agreement?
questions.stem_ja: 契約後のメラの立場が一長一短である理由は何か。

choices.text: Its membership gave it equal patent rights but fewer engineering resources.
choices.text_ja: 参加したことで同等の特許権を得たが、技術的な資源は少なかったから。

choices.text: A license simplified manufacturing, but no compatible interface was available.
choices.text_ja: ライセンスによって製造は簡単になったが、互換性のあるインターフェースがなかったから。

choices.text: A common interface simplified design, but access to covered technology remained costly.
choices.text_ja: 共通インターフェースによって設計は簡単になったが、対象技術を使うための費用は依然として高かったから。

choices.text: The standard removed fees but required Mera to design two separate controllers.
choices.text_ja: 規格によって料金はなくなったが、メラは二種類の別々の制御装置を設計しなければならなかったから。

questions.stem: Why is an increase in compatible products insufficient evidence of stronger overall competition?
questions.stem_ja: 互換性のある製品が増えたことが、全体として競争が強まったことの証拠として不十分なのはなぜか。

choices.text: The count may rise among signatories while access conditions discourage outside designs.
choices.text_ja: 契約した企業の間で製品の数が増えても、利用条件のために外部からの設計が妨げられているかもしれないから。

choices.text: The products might differ in service quality even when their interfaces match.
choices.text_ja: インターフェースが一致していても、製品のサービスの質は異なるかもしれないから。

choices.text: The original disputes provide a more direct measure of customer benefits.
choices.text_ja: もとの争いのほうが、顧客の利益をより直接的に測る尺度になるから。

choices.text: Compatibility prevents customers from choosing between the two firms.
choices.text_ja: 互換性があると、顧客は二社のどちらかを選べなくなるから。

questions.stem: Which change would most directly address Mera's concern while preserving compensation for development?
questions.stem_ja: 開発への対価を維持しつつ、メラの懸念に最も直接的に対処する変更はどれか。

choices.text: Require Mera to supply an alternative connection design in exchange for access to the standard.
choices.text_ja: 規格を使う許可と引き換えに、メラに別の接続方式の設計を提供させる。

choices.text: Set the same large initial fee for each applicant and judge openness by approvals granted.
choices.text_ja: すべての申請者に同じ高額の初期料金を課し、承認件数で開放性を判断する。

choices.text: Offer transparent, consistently applied access terms that account for the cost faced by entrants.
choices.text_ja: 新規参入者が負う費用を考慮した、透明で一貫して適用される利用条件を示す。

choices.text: Increase compatible additions within the agreement and use their sales to set outside fees.
choices.text_ja: 契約の範囲内で互換性のある追加製品を増やし、その売上をもとに外部向けの料金を決める。

questions.stem: What is the central reason for making two comparisons across time?
questions.stem_ja: 時間をまたいだ二つの比較を行う主な理由は何か。

choices.text: The earlier incompatible products are no longer relevant once the standard exists.
choices.text_ja: 規格ができれば、以前の互換性のない製品はもはや関係がなくなるから。

choices.text: The same agreement can change insiders' and outsiders' opportunities differently.
choices.text_ja: 同じ契約でも、内側の企業と外側の企業の機会を異なる形で変えうるから。

choices.text: Customers and entrants measure success with identical evidence.
choices.text_ja: 顧客と新規参入者は、まったく同じ証拠で成功を測るから。

choices.text: The number of signatories is a better outcome measure than product development.
choices.text_ja: 契約した企業の数のほうが、製品開発よりも優れた成果の指標だから。

passage.title: Why Flexible Pipes Can Survive Shaking

paragraphs.text: During an imagined repair after an earthquake, workers uncover a water pipe beneath a road that has shifted sideways. The pipe body looks largely intact, but a connection has separated. Nearby, another section has changed angle without coming apart. The contrast challenges an everyday idea of strength: that the hardest or most rigid object should be the most resistant to damage. For an underground pipeline, survival also depends on how its parts respond when the ground around them does not move together.

A buried pipe interacts with soil along its route. If one section of ground moves differently from the next, the pipe may be stretched, compressed, or bent. A joint that allows little relative movement can concentrate the resulting demand at a narrow location. A strong pipe body does not prevent a weaker connection from opening, and making the body more rigid does not necessarily make the whole line better able to follow ground deformation. The relevant unit of analysis is the connected system, including its surroundings.

A joint designed for controlled movement offers another response. Within its intended range, it may allow rotation or some extension while maintaining the connection and its seal. Instead of demanding that the ground remain aligned, the system accommodates a limited change in alignment. This is not the same as leaving the connection loose. The movement must be compatible with continued water pressure and with the forces that tend to pull sections apart. Useful flexibility therefore includes both freedom to move and constraints that preserve the function of the connection.

Ground conditions determine how much movement that design may need to accommodate. Shaking can produce temporary motion, but settlement or other lasting displacement can leave adjacent sections in new positions. Soft or unstable ground may introduce demands unlike those in a firm site used for a demonstration. A flexible joint that performs well under repeated small movements may reach its limit during a large permanent shift. It is therefore misleading to describe a joint as earthquake-resistant without asking which movement patterns and surrounding conditions were considered.

Imagine two proposed systems for the same route. One has a stronger rigid pipe body but connections with a smaller movement range. The other has connections that permit more controlled movement, although its suitability still depends on pressure, installation, and soil interaction. If the main expected difficulty is relative movement between ground sections, the second design may offer an advantage. If its permitted movement is exceeded, however, that advantage cannot simply be assumed to continue. Comparing the word 'stronger' with the word 'flexible' hides the quantities a designer actually needs.

Testing should consequently examine both motion and function. A sample that bends without breaking but loses its seal has not met the same requirement as a sample that remains connected and carries water. Tests should represent the direction, size, and repetition of expected movement as far as practical. Results from one arrangement also need careful interpretation when applied to another: support conditions, the distance between joints, and installation details can alter how demand is distributed. A successful component test is valuable evidence, but it is not a complete demonstration of an entire network's performance.

Returning to the repair, the separated joint and the bent intact section are clues rather than a controlled experiment. They may have experienced different soil movement, installation quality, or loads. Investigators should examine those differences before assigning the outcome solely to the type of joint. The example nevertheless identifies the right question: how did each section manage the displacement imposed on it, and which function was lost when its capacity was exceeded?

Flexible connections can improve resilience by accommodating movement that would otherwise concentrate damage, provided that their range and other requirements match the situation. Material strength remains necessary, but it is one part of the design. A pipeline's ability to survive shaking is better understood as a relationship among strength, movement capacity, connections, and ground behavior than as a contest to select the hardest material.

questions.stem: Why is the intact pipe body beside a separated joint significant?
questions.stem_ja: 外れた継ぎ目のそばにある無傷の管本体は、なぜ重要なのか。

choices.text: It shows that pipe-body strength is a reliable substitute for measuring connection performance.
choices.text_ja: 管本体の強さが、継ぎ目の性能を測ることの信頼できる代わりになることを示しているから。

choices.text: It shows how failure of a connection can determine the system's performance.
choices.text_ja: 継ぎ目の破損がシステムの性能を左右しうることを示しているから。

choices.text: It proves that rigid materials caused both observed outcomes.
choices.text_ja: 硬い材料が、観察された両方の結果を引き起こしたことを証明しているから。

choices.text: It identifies installation quality as the main cause of the contrast with the intact section.
choices.text_ja: 無傷の区間との違いの主な原因として、施工品質を特定しているから。

questions.stem: What distinguishes controlled joint movement from simple looseness?
questions.stem_ja: 制御された継ぎ目の動きは、単なる緩さとどこが違うのか。

choices.text: Controlled movement keeps the ground aligned with the original pipe route.
choices.text_ja: 制御された動きは、地盤を元の管の経路に沿った状態に保つ。

choices.text: Controlled movement permits displacement within limits while preserving connection and sealing.
choices.text_ja: 制御された動きは、つながりと水密性を保ちながら、一定の範囲内で変位を許す。

choices.text: Controlled movement is assessed by visible bending rather than water delivery.
choices.text_ja: 制御された動きは、水を届けられるかどうかではなく、目に見える曲がりによって評価される。

choices.text: Controlled movement makes sealing less relevant than bending capacity.
choices.text_ja: 制御された動きにより、水密性は曲がる能力よりも重要でなくなる。

questions.stem: When would the second proposed system's movement capacity be most relevant to its advantage?
questions.stem_ja: 二つ目に提案されたシステムの動きへの対応能力が、その有利さに最も関係するのはどのような場合か。

choices.text: When pressure performance is uncertain but its joints visibly bend more.
choices.text_ja: 水圧に対する性能は不確かだが、継ぎ目が目に見えてより大きく曲がる場合。

choices.text: When small repeated test movements replace consideration of permanent ground shifts.
choices.text_ja: 小さな動きを繰り返す試験が、永続的な地盤のずれの検討に取って代わる場合。

choices.text: When expected relative ground movement falls within its controlled range and other requirements are met.
choices.text_ja: 予想される地盤の相対的な動きが制御された範囲内に収まり、その他の要件も満たされている場合。

choices.text: When its pipe body is described as less rigid, regardless of the expected displacement.
choices.text_ja: 予想される変位にかかわらず、管本体がより硬くないと説明される場合。

questions.stem: Which result most directly limits a claim that a tested system remained functional?
questions.stem_ja: 試験したシステムが機能を保ったという主張を最も直接的に制限するのは、どの結果か。

choices.text: It accommodated movement without fracture but lost water through the joint.
choices.text_ja: 破断せずに動きを受け止めたが、継ぎ目から水が漏れた。

choices.text: Its movement capacity was stated for a particular direction and range.
choices.text_ja: 動きへの対応能力が、特定の方向と範囲について示されていた。

choices.text: It changed angle while remaining connected under the test conditions.
choices.text_ja: 試験条件のもとで、つながったまま角度が変わった。

choices.text: Its supports differed from those of another tested arrangement.
choices.text_ja: 支持の条件が、別に試験された配置のものと異なっていた。

questions.stem: Why compare ground and installation conditions before explaining the two repair outcomes?
questions.stem_ja: 修理現場の二つの結果を説明する前に、なぜ地盤と施工の条件を比較するのか。

choices.text: The visible damage can be used to reconstruct ground movement without checking the surrounding soil.
choices.text_ja: 目に見える損傷から、周囲の土を調べなくても地盤の動きを再構成できるから。

choices.text: An intact section provides less useful evidence than a damaged one.
choices.text_ja: 無傷の区間は、損傷した区間よりも役に立たない証拠しか与えないから。

choices.text: Successful component tests provide the common exposure needed to compare the two field sections.
choices.text_ja: 部品試験の成功が、現場の二つの区間を比較するのに必要な共通の条件を与えるから。

choices.text: Different demands could explain the contrast even if joint design also matters.
choices.text_ja: 継ぎ目の設計も重要だとしても、受けた負荷の違いがその対比を説明しうるから。

passage.title: The Long Life of a Short-Lived Fashion

paragraphs.text: Bright jackets fill the sorting room in the fictional town of Brindle. They were popular for one season, and many still look almost new. A local resale cooperative sees an opportunity: repair the damaged fastenings, find new owners, and keep useful clothing in use. Its first report celebrates the number of jackets sold again. The figure records a real achievement in handling unwanted goods, but a volunteer asks a harder question. How many of those sales changed what people bought, rather than simply adding another inexpensive jacket to their wardrobes?

Across town, a shop is preparing the next fashionable color. Some customers now buy with resale in mind, expecting to recover part of the price when they move on. This expectation can make an item feel less costly to own briefly. In Brindle's imagined case, several interviewed shoppers say that reliable resale encourages them to replace jackets sooner. Their comments do not establish what every customer does, but they identify a possible link between an efficient secondhand market and the continued speed of new purchases.

Back in the sorting room, practical work determines which garments have another useful life. A missing button may be easy to replace; damage to a specialized fastening may require more time or a part the cooperative cannot obtain. Staff separate ready-to-wear items from those needing repair and from those unlikely to sell. The distinction matters because a donated jacket is not yet a worn jacket. Counting everything received as successful reuse would skip the work and uncertainty between donation and another person's actual use.

The cooperative tries a repair service that owners can use before donating. One customer brings back a jacket with a broken zip and keeps it for another season. That outcome produces no resale transaction, yet it may extend use just as meaningfully as a second sale. It also avoids the need to find a new buyer for that particular garment. Whether it reduces environmental impact still depends partly on what the owner would otherwise have done, but the case shows why transaction totals can miss valuable forms of continued use.

Some sorted stock is sent to a distant partner because local demand is limited. Transport and further sorting require resources, and an item accepted by the partner may still remain unsold. Distance alone does not establish that the transfer is wasteful: a jacket that reaches someone who uses it instead of buying new may produce a different result from one stored or discarded after the trip. The cooperative therefore asks for information about final use rather than treating departure from its own warehouse as the end of the story.

Comparing two hypothetical buyers makes the central distinction clearer. One buys a used jacket instead of a planned new purchase and wears it regularly. Another buys the same kind of used jacket as an extra while continuing an unchanged pattern of new purchases. Both generate one secondhand sale, but the first offers stronger evidence that new demand has been displaced. Even then, a single avoided purchase does not directly measure a factory's production response. The chain from household choice to total material use contains further steps that should be investigated rather than assumed.

Brindle revises its assessment to follow repair outcomes, use after sale, and changes in purchasing habits alongside the number of transactions. Interviews and follow-up reports have limits, including incomplete responses, so the cooperative presents them as evidence about likely pathways rather than an exact environmental total. It also separates garments kept in use from garments merely transferred elsewhere. This approach makes the report less dramatic but more useful for deciding where repair effort, buyer information, and distribution work have the greatest value.

The jackets can outlast the fashion that brought them into the shops. Whether that longer material life reduces the burden of producing and moving clothing depends on the consumption it supports or replaces. Resale, repair, and transport each belong in the account, as do the new purchases made alongside them. A successful secondhand system gives clothing further opportunities for use; evaluating its wider benefit requires following what people do with those opportunities.

passage.title: The City That Wakes Before Its Animals

paragraphs.text: Before sunrise, delivery engines begin to interrupt the quieter sounds of a city street. A lamp still shines over a patch of pavement, while a nearby park path remains dark. To a worker starting an early shift, both places belong to the same morning. For animals, however, that clock label says little about the conditions they encounter. Light, noise, temperature, and available food can change on different schedules. The ecological setting includes not only where a creature can go, but when a place becomes usable.

From the perspective of insects, a lamp can change the distribution of activity. Some insects gather around artificial lights, concentrating in a small area rather than remaining spread across darker surroundings. A large count at the lamp therefore need not mean that the neighborhood contains more insects overall. It may reflect movement toward a visible source. Nor does attraction demonstrate a benefit to the insects: time spent around a light can differ from the activities they would otherwise perform. The observer sees a concentration, while its broader consequences require another kind of evidence.

For an insect-eating bat, that concentration may offer a feeding opportunity. Some bats forage near lamps, but others avoid illuminated areas or alter the routes they use. Even a species seen feeding in light may be affected differently when light falls on its route from a resting place. A successful feeding observation at one lamp cannot therefore be extended to a claim that bright nights improve conditions for bats generally. The activity being performed and the species involved both change the meaning of exposure.

The worker's needs add a third perspective. Deliveries and cleaning must be organized around access, visibility, and other people using the street. A proposal to change the timing of a lamp may affect those tasks. But keeping the same lighting schedule throughout the night is also a choice, not a neutral background. In a hypothetical planning discussion, workers might identify periods when light is essential at a loading entrance, while ecologists identify a nearby dark route used by animals. The question becomes whether lighting and timing can be adjusted to serve distinct uses without assuming that one schedule suits the entire area.

Season complicates that discussion. The hour on a clock may remain the same while its relation to sunrise or sunset changes. Insect availability and animal activity can also vary with temperature and season. A bat recorded later by the clock in one month may not have shifted its behavior relative to darkness by the same amount. Comparing observations therefore requires more than noting the time displayed on a recorder. Weather, daylight, and the local schedule of lighting and traffic help define the conditions associated with the activity.

Light and noise should likewise be distinguished rather than grouped under the word urban. Suppose a hypothetical monitoring project finds fewer bat passes after an early delivery period begins. Engines, headlights, people, and changing natural light may all overlap in that interval. The observation identifies a pattern worth investigating, but it does not isolate a cause. Comparing nights or locations where those factors differ could help test explanations. Observers would also need to consider whether a change in recorded passes reflects animals using another route, altered detection, or a change in numbers.

That final distinction is essential for judging outcomes. An animal appearing at a different hour or place may have reorganized its activity without the local population changing. Conversely, apparent activity around a lamp may conceal reduced access elsewhere. Following a fuller daily cycle and examining different routes gives a more informative picture than concentrating on the busiest visible spot. Information about population change requires evidence beyond the timing of a few encounters.

The early worker and the feeding bat thus inhabit overlapping schedules as well as overlapping space. Understanding their city means mapping when conditions change and whose activities those changes permit or interrupt. It does not require a single story in which animals simply become more nocturnal or adapt successfully to human routines. A city's time pattern is part of its habitat, and its effects must be examined with the same care as its physical layout.

passage.title: The Cemetery That Moved with the Town

paragraphs.text: During the final communal cleaning at the old cemetery, residents of the fictional village of Harrowbank brush moss from stones and clear the paths between them. A planned reservoir will cover the valley, and the village is moving to higher ground. The relocation plan includes a new cemetery with carefully numbered plots. Officials describe how stones and remains will be transferred under an agreed process. On paper, the proposal appears to preserve what matters. Standing among the old paths, some families are less certain.

The argument for relocation is substantial. Leaving the cemetery in place would expose it to the reservoir project and make visits difficult or impossible. The new site would provide access from the relocated village, maintained paths, and space for future burials. Officials have consulted families about handling the move respectfully. These practical protections should not be dismissed simply because relocation involves loss. For residents who chiefly fear being unable to visit relatives' graves, a reachable and cared-for site offers something important that remaining in the valley would not.

Other residents object to describing the move as complete preservation. A grave's position may carry associations with a nearby tree, an old house visible across the valley, or the route taken during family visits. The order of plots can also express relationships that a tidy new numbering system fails to show. Even if every stone arrives undamaged, those connections do not automatically travel with it. This objection concerns the limits of the officials' claim, rather than necessarily opposing the physical protection the move would provide.

A local historian proposes detailed recording before the valley changes. Photographs, a plan of the plots, and accounts of how people used the paths could preserve information that individual stones do not contain. Families add names for informal sections and explain why certain visits followed a particular sequence. The historian distinguishes these recorded accounts from a complete reconstruction of experience. A map can show where a tree stood; it cannot reproduce the shade of that tree during a visit. Documentation can retain knowledge while acknowledging what it cannot replace.

The relocation committee then revises parts of the design. Where practical, neighboring family plots will remain near one another. A gathering space will allow the community to continue its shared cleaning day, and the old plan will be available at the new site. Families can contribute memories without being required to agree on one explanation of the cemetery's meaning. Some prefer a joint ceremony before the move; others want private observances. The committee makes room for both rather than treating one visible ritual as evidence that everyone has accepted the same interpretation.

These changes produce partial agreement. Several families who criticized the original description now support the revised arrangements, while still saying that something irreplaceable will be lost. A few remain opposed to the relocation itself. Officials could report the number of families approving the practical plan, but presenting that number as proof that community memory had been preserved would go further than the evidence. Consent to a workable response under difficult circumstances is different from believing that the response restores everything valued at the old location.

The historian suggests evaluating the project through several questions after the move. Are graves accessible and maintained? Can families identify the old relationships among plots? Do people continue the practices they wanted to carry forward? Which connections remain difficult to express? These questions avoid a single success label based solely on the safe arrival of objects. They also prevent the opposite mistake of declaring every effort meaningless because the original valley cannot be retained.

Harrowbank's cemetery moves with the village in a physical and administrative sense, but its continuity must also be made through records, practices, and relationships. The residents do not share one view of what has survived, and their disagreement is part of the history being preserved. A defensible account recognizes the protection achieved and the losses that remain. Preservation here means caring for several kinds of connection, without pretending that moving the stones moves the entire place.
